#5792. Thermal Dawn — Thermal Storage Is Cheap Storage

Another great idea from Down Under: Thermal Dawn promises cost effective heating and cooling, mainly by replacing gas boilers in cold climates. CleanTechnica had a chance to interview Nick Zeniou, Founder of Thermal Dawn, recently by phone, fresh after his presentation at Everything Electric. You can hear him explain his revolutionary system here, or here with a little less drama.

Everything Electric was a good opportunity to measure public reaction to the new product. Nick tells me that hundreds of people checked out their stall. “People care about carbon cost and comfort. People don’t compromise on comfort.” Sounds like comfort trumps carbon cost. Homeowners who visited the stand and filled out the survey were focused on sustainability and cost. Nick cautions: “it was an electrification expo crowd, and 50 of the 62 already had solar, so it’s not the whole market.” See the chart below.

Although I live in the warmer part of Australia (Brisbane), many Aussies have to endure cold winters. Nick tells me he is looking at installs in Sydney, Canberra, and Melbourne in the deep south. Thermal Dawn can store heat up to 70 degrees Celsius, or down to 5 degrees. Thermal Dawns’ equipment can run cold or hot water through pipes and radiators that are already installed, depending on the need — without having to run an expensive gas boiler. He describes it as a thermal battery. Just to be clear, it does not generate electricity.

Check out this graph below, which shows the Thermal Dawn system in action at a house in Melbourne during a day in August 2026. It shows room temperature and when the heat pump was running, in 15-minute samples, unedited. The heat pump ran until about 1:45pm, then not again, heated by stored energy through the evening peak.

“What about return on investment,” I asked. He described two systems they have had running over the southern Australian winter which have saved the homeowners approximately AU$1,500 each. “The first was a house in Melbourne, our first install, live since May 2026. The owners charge the system in their retailer’s free three-hour midday window, so the heat for the evening costs them close to nothing. The second was a Warragul (slab-heated home, Victoria): installed in two days in July 2026. Our controls turn the home’s concrete slab into part of the battery, managing when it charges and when it releases heat. On 95% of winter evenings, the heat pumps did not run at all between 5 pm and 9pm. Since commissioning, 70,521 MJ of gas has been avoided by just these two installations.”

Nick further explains: “A standard heat pump draws from the grid during those expensive morning and evening hours. You’ve escaped gas, but you’re still paying premium rates every time the temperature drops at night. Thermal Dawn is different. Our system charges when power is cheapest, a free midday window, your own solar, or late-night off-peak, then delivers that stored warmth through your radiators and underfloor heating all evening, with the compressor off through the expensive hours.

It appears that Thermal Dawn’s secret sauce is “Phase Change Materials.” Naturally, Nick declined to share exactly what Thermal Dawn is using. The system replaces a gas boiler with a combination of reverse cycle heat pump, well insulated water tank, and phase change materials. PCMs are designed to freeze or melt at a specific temperature, storing and releasing heat when they change physical state, usually from solid to liquid. “PCM doubles our heat capacity.” The heating applications I could understand, what about the cooling? “Cool water from the tank runs through a fan coil unit, and the fan blows cool air into the room. Cooling is an optional add-on.” That’s the answer.

How do thermal storage and a home battery/solar system work together? “Thermal storage is cheap storage doing one job very well. Heating, cooling, and hot water are the largest, most predictable loads in the house, and covering them thermally is far cheaper per kWh than covering them from lithium. A battery is expensive storage doing a general-purpose job.

“The practical effect is that your battery stops being the thing that carries your heating. It’s freed up for lights, appliances, the EV, and overnight backup, and it lasts longer for not being cycled hard every winter evening. Homes with a battery already are often the clearest case, because the expensive storage stops being spent on the cheapest possible job.”

Thermal dawn connects to existing hydronic pipework. The gas boiler with its high gas bills is gone. Check out the animation of heat discharge overnight. “The thermal battery charged on solar during the day and now heats the house while the heat pump stays off. It’s an illustration of what the app shows, not a recording of a live home.” For those rooms that don’t have hydronic radiators or underfloor slab heating, Thermal Dawn installs fan coil units. Nick tells me via a followup email that: “It’s a small indoor unit with a water coil and a fan: warm water from the thermal battery runs through the coil, and the fan blows the heating or cooling into the room.”

The heavy technical discussion out of the way, I asked Nick about his background. He grew up in an isolated part of New Zealand. His job was to collect the firewood for the family’s heat source — a fireplace. He had to get the fire going by 4:00 pm or the house would not warm up for the cold evening. Timing was very important, as it is for electricity use.

Nick is a mechanical engineer who has worked across tech companies and startups. While working on installing commercial air conditioning, he came across the idea that became Thermal Dawn. Nick joined the dots between the huge variations in electricity supply cost throughout each 24-hour period, with an average home’s thermal energy needs (up to two-thirds of consumption) and the fact that homes are becoming power stations. Thence to thermal batteries powered by Thermal Dawn technology.

He reminisces about the start of the business: “When our first unit was finished, we loaded it into a ute at 5pm and I drove it down the Hume overnight, Sydney to Melbourne (1000 km), to install it the next morning. We had a four-month-old at home at the time. My wife Linda is my co-founder and leads mechanical design and manufacturing, so while I was on the road, she was looking after a newborn.”

For those who would like to get involved, Nick invites Australian homeowners to sign up here and they’ll be in touch. “Readers overseas: send us a message or request a quote at the same link to register interest. If we hear from enough people in one area, we can bring forward our plans to come there.”

Having proven their point, Thermal Dawn is cleared to sell and installing its first batch now, with a larger product for ducted air conditioning in development. I asked about apartment block heating and Nick confirmed that they are looking at it but want to get the domestic home sorted first.

I asked a couple of followup questions “What about the Victorian government’s position?” Nick’s answer:  “Victoria is set to bring in support for systems like ours from the middle of next year. With the state election in November, there’s talk of a change in direction and of belt-tightening, so we’ve built Thermal Dawn to stand on its own. It saves households money without a subsidy, and any support is a bonus.”

Any plans for installs in Canberra? “Yes. Canberra is one of the best places in Australia for this: cold winters, plenty of hydronic homes, and a territory already moving off gas. We’re talking with installers there now.”

I really appreciate these technological experts when they take the time to explain things to me. Sometimes I feel like Winnie the Pooh — a bear of very little brain. Looks like Thermal Dawn has solved another part of the energy puzzle — good news for homeowners and also for the planet.

David Waterworth is a retired teacher who divides his time between looking after his grandchildren and trying to make sure they have a planet to live on. He is long on Tesla [NASDAQ:TSLA].

#5791. How Can Europe Accelerate Electric Trucking?

Europe is having a hard time lately, with skyrocketing oil prices dampening economies. Fuel costs, particularly diesel, are prompting surging interest in truck electrification. Europe has been urging truck makers to move toward electric trucking, and they have responded with a variety of electric semi trucks from many manufacturers. Europe is a group of sovereign countries with many standards. The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 states in that area. It issued directives urging action and imposing penalties. In response to European Union directives, companies have formed EV100, a coalition of corporations responding to the need. In a recent story, Steve Hanley wrote about European electric truck makers’ difficulties expanding truck electrification. Here’s a quotation from the story: “In a letter to EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, of primary concern, in their estimation, is expanding the charging infrastructure for heavy-duty trucks in Europe.” There is no shortage of electric trucks in Europe. Expansion could go faster were it not for charging infrastructure. Manufacturers complain about “an alarming delay” in conditions needed to drive market uptake. For Europe, truck electrification is not working as well as in China, where over 90% of the world’s electric trucks reside. The differences between China and the EU show some reasons why truck electrification is slower in Europe. How did China succeed where the EU failed? China made electric trucks a freight system, not a vehicle category.

Power is a major factor in electric grid infrastructure. Charging electric trucks places demands on power. Peak power determines how much infrastructure is necessary. In grid planning, peak annual power determines how much capital equipment is necessary. Reducing peak power demand is a critical factor for electric truck infrastructure. Figure 1 shows one method of reducing power called route stuffing. It schedules departures on heavy traffic corridors at regularly spaced intervals. Corridors like ones between ports and warehouses are a target for those practices. These corridors often route trucks in a round trip chain. Filling routes with scheduled trips can reduce power demand compared to random trip scheduling. The article Battery Swap Uses Fewer Batteries Than You Think is devoted to methods of analysis and planning that can lead to lower peak power demand. There are other benefits to planning, such as greater truck load capacity from the same amount of batteries. Part of the solution to slow electric truck infrastructure development is to plan infrastructure and truck use practices to reduce the charging power burden. Given the pressing and enduring need due to the diesel fuel cost crisis, it is necessary to reprioritize grid power upgrade demands. Demands for data center power upgrades like transformers for substations should be re shuffled and prioritized toward the diesel crisis.

In two articles, Michael Barnard outlined the issues. Vehicles are not a transportation system. What does Europe have now? It has an EU Commission interacting with a coalition, EV100. The problem is, there are plenty of trucks available, but who is in charge of infrastructure? You can’t have electric trucks without means of charging, but as the coalition complains, “Significant improvements to charging infrastructure, a reduction in carbon dioxide based tolls, and a coherent policy framework are urgently needed.” There are so many stakeholders — including the commission, vehicles makers, and charging companies across multiple countries — that no one is in charge of infrastructure, and without it, nothing moves. It needs a unity of purpose and action.

If China is succeeding, why not adopt its strategy? Perhaps the answer is right in front of everyone’s nose. As Michael puts it, “the policy connects vehicles to corridors, depots, service areas, grids and freight use cases instead of treating sales targets as sufficient.” CATL offered Europe a system, not a vehicle. This is a “turn key” solution. It’s a well thought out system, including use of methods and practices, not an anything goes free-for-all. That kind of stability and predictability is what EV100 leaders are looking for. This is not a swap-or-nothing scenario. Different techniques apply to various use cases. Swap must be planned for high-use freight corridors and other proper applications. Swap trucks can also fast charge or slow charge, providing flexibility and a system of trucks that includes smaller trucks, not just semis.

What does all this have to do with Europe’s slowly advancing infrastructure? Simply put, electric trucks put heavy charging demands on the grid. Trucks can have megawatt-hour batteries that require megawatt power charging to charge in an hour. Reducing grid power demands can reduce grid infrastructure upgrade costs, and leverage capital investment toward faster implementation.

“The process of getting megawatt charging equipment connected to the grid can take several years, delaying deployment even where operators and infrastructure providers are ready to invest.” The need for megawatt charging equipment is reduced by accelerating swap network development instead of fixed battery trucks that must be charged by fast chargers. “Swaptopus is easy to misread as a quirky name for another electric-truck infrastructure project. It is a newly formed joint venture between Octopus Energy and CATL, created to develop automated battery-swapping hubs for heavy trucks across Europe.” Unlike the government of China that played a role in encouraging standards and cooperation in infrastructure, Europe has a looser arrangement between many countries with various standards. Europe is learning the slow, hard way where battery swapping is most needed.

Every truck application has different optimization. It means that there must be different approaches to fit freight operations in heavy traffic corridors. Quoting Michael Barnard, “Freight operators often run repeated routes between ports, factories, distribution centres and logistics hubs. Those patterns provide known traffic, known stopping points and relatively predictable electricity demand. A swap hub can be placed around an existing freight flow instead of hoping that enough unrelated trucks eventually pass through.”

Freight corridors are a scenario made to order for battery swap. Real trucking solutions include a mix of vehicle and infrastructure types — from small, local delivery, to large, long-haul freight; and from slow, overnight charging, to medium power charging and battery swap — all used in concert to accelerate heavy truck electrification. With a wide variety of charging options, and vehicles and charging use cases targeted in coordination to avoid peak power demands, the path forward is eased. School buses don’t need expensive high-power fast charging. Lower-power chargers can do the trick. Local delivery can use a mix of overnight and medium power charging. Heavy truck dispatch must be more carefully coordinated to avoid peak demand and grid upgrade costs. A mix of medium-power charging and swap stations along with planned use cases can successfully lower electric freight power needs and transport system capital expenses to speed transport electrification.

Transformation and conversion of diesel freight systems to electric requires coordination and planning between government agencies and coalitions of corporations, cities, government agencies, and planners. Transportation is a system basic to societies and economics. Coordination between groups at all levels results in practices, use cases, and infrastructure that produce benefits for all. Grid expansion and construction can take years. In order for Europe to implement truck freight electrification, more structure and planning is needed to minimize grid power requirements, speed implementation, and maximize capital investment results. Transportation system, practices, and infrastructure must be planned for optimum results.

#5790. 'ER' and 'The Pitt' Similar Enough for Lawsuit to Move Forward, Appeals Court Says

— The lawsuit was filed 2 years ago by the "ER" creator's wife and estate

A California appeals court has found that "ER" and "The Pitt" have enough similarity that a lawsuit brought by the widow and estate of "ER" creator Michael Crichton alleging "The Pitt" is an unauthorized reboot can move forward.

A three-judge panel from California's 2nd District Court of Appeal ruled unanimously on Wednesday that the trial court judge was correct to reject a motion to throw out the case from "The Pitt" production company Warner Bros. Television, which also produced "ER." But the judges dismissed Noah Wyle -- the star of both shows and a producer on "The Pitt" -- as a defendant along with two other producers who worked on both series.

The lawsuit is a clash between the makers of multiple Emmy-winning TV series that were each among the most important and acclaimed shows of their eras.

Crichton, the author of "Jurassic Park" and many other novels that became hit movies and TV shows, wrote the pilot script for "ER," the NBC show about a Chicago emergency room that redefined the medical drama genre and drew tens of millions of weekly viewers in its run from 1994 to 2009.

The lawsuit brought by Sherri Crichton was filed 2 years ago, before a single episode of "The Pitt" had aired. The HBO Max series that shows a real-time day in the life of a Pittsburgh emergency department has since become perhaps the most lauded series in television, winning two Emmys for best drama for its first two seasons and two best actor Emmys for Wyle.

Along with more technical legal issues, the judges had to decide whether the shows had at least the minimal similarity that would give the lawsuit enough merit to move forward. Their decision applies only to this early legal challenge and they did not rule on whether the plaintiffs had proved that "The Pitt" is derivative of "ER."

The court agreed with the plaintiff that "both shows provide commentaries on the healthcare system; they focus specifically on the emergency room and the difficult conditions under which the medical staff operates. Both shows take place, with little exception, in the emergency room, as opposed to other medical shows which track patients as they move out of the emergency room, or indeed never enter it."

The opinion also said that both feature "very fast pacing, and reactions to multiple overlapping crises. The fast-paced dialogue is (to a layperson) frequently incomprehensible shorthand and jargon, lending an air of immediacy and accuracy."

Warner Bros. Television said in a statement that "WBTV continues to maintain that 'The Pitt' is an entirely original series and that the claims against it are without merit. Nothing in the Court of Appeal's decision establishes otherwise, and WBTV looks forward to defending its position as the case proceeds."

The defendants argued in legal filings that the shows have "generic similarities" that would exist in "any dramatic story" that features "overworked doctors and staff."

The panel also unanimously dismissed as defendants Wyle; John Wells, who created "The Pitt" and worked on "ER"; and R. Scott Gemmill, a "Pitt" executive producer who also worked on both shows. The judges found there was no evidence the three men knew the provisions of the Crichton contract that the lawsuit alleges they interfered with.

Sherri Crichton's lawsuit alleges "The Pitt" is a rebranded version of an unauthorized "ER" reboot that she had rejected.

Her husband had secured a coveted "frozen rights" provision in his contract for the series, prohibiting Warner Bros. from proceeding with any sequels, remakes, spinoffs, or other productions derived from "ER" without Crichton's consent, or his estate's consent after his death from cancer in 2008.

After the production company could not reach an agreement with Sherri Crichton over a proposed "ER" reboot, the TV studio proceeded to develop and produce a series based on the same premise without permission, the lawsuit alleges.

#5789. Trump Is Gonna Cave On Offshore Wind In 5…4…3…

…JK! US President Donald Trump will never cry surrender in the war against offshore wind turbines. The President was burned once before, when a wind farm arose in Aberdeen Bay in Scotland, within view of a Trump-branded golf course back in the early 2000’s. Never again! The President has taken extreme measures to prevent such blight from tainting the shores of the United States. Nevertheless, scores of the pesky oversized pinwheels have already eluded the Trump chopper, and many more are on the way.

The latest news concerns CVOW, the 2.6-gigwatt Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project under the wing of the leading utility Dominion. As the name of the project indicates, CVOW sits in the Atlantic Ocean about 24 nautical miles (28 land miles) off the coast of Virginia Beach, Virginia.

CVOW began taking shape during Trump’s first turn around the Oval Office, and construction was well under way when his second term began on January 20, 2025.

Immediately upon taking office, Trump abruptly suspended the offshore wind lease program administered by the Department of the Interior. He also ordered spurious re-reviews of offshore projects that were already in the permitting pipeline, and he had the Department of Justice administer a legally questionable buy-back program to prevent activity from stirring among other lease holders. In addition, he had the Interior Department issue multiple emergency orders aimed at stopping five offshore projects off the coasts of Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, Maryland, and Massachusetts, where construction work was already well under way.

So far, though, only one part of the effort has stuck. Last year a federal judge affirmed that any President, Trump or not, has the authority to stop issuing new offshore leases. However, the same judge decided there is no blanket authority to suspend offshore leases that are already in the permitting process. The buy-back program is also in litigation, with critics raising questions about the funds used to pay off lease holders among other issues.

Additionally,  the Interior Department failed to convince multiple federal judges that the emergency orders had any merit. Work has continued on all five Atlantic coast projects, including CVOW.

CVOW began delivering its first kilowatts to shore in March, and Dominion recapped its progress on the wind farm in its Q3 report on October 30. As handily summarized by the news organization Maritime Executive, the project currently clocks in at 85% complete. All of the main turbine components — nacelles, towers, and blades — for the wind farm’s 176 offshore wind turbines have been fabricated. Forty-four have been fully installed so far. With a 45th coming any day now, the wind farm currently hosts 640 megawatts out of the 2,600 megawatt total.

Since Trump declared an “Energy Emergency” in January of 2025, it’s fair to ask why he has spent so much time, energy and taxpayer dollars to crush an entire domestic energy industry. After all, if one was not reading too closely between the lines of the declaration, the new energy policy is little more than a rehash of former President Barack Obama’s “All Of The Above” energy policy. As further embellished by Energy Secretary Chris Wright, the new version specifically taps multiple zero and low-emission energy resources for support including nuclear energy, biomass, hydropower, and geothermal energy, just like Obama did, along the emerging field of marine energy, which was barely a speck on the horizon while Obama was in office.

Energy storage, and the critical minerals needed in the clean tech industry, have also been gathered up in a Trumpian embrace.

Conspicuously absent, however, are the two most abundant, economical, and easily accessible domestic energy resources, namely, wind and solar.

If there really was an energy emergency…oh, never mind! Despite Trump’s complaints, offshore wind is a mature industry with a vigorous supply global supply chain and support equipment, as deftly illustrated by the CVOW project. In the October 30 report, Dominion noted that it takes only about two days for an offshore construction vessel to install a wind turbine on its foundation.

While the offshore wind construction timetable is subject to weather delays, Dominion also stated that the project is on schedule — despite any further delays related to last year’s stop-work order.

Speaking of the stop-work order, CVOW was conspicuously excluded from previous rounds of stop-work orders impacting the four other Atlantic coast wind farms under construction in 2025. If you’re guessing that Virginia’s Republican Governor, Glenn Youngkin, had a hand in that decision, drop a note in the discussion thread. Youngkin publicly supported the CVOW project but he was term-limited out of office last year. A stop-work order would have put an embarrassing crimp in his next-step political plans. The order came down only after Election Day 2025, after the Democratic candidate, Abigail Spanberger, won the post.

In a classic case of karma biting back, CVOW is a  more efficient and economical project than initially envisioned. A round of delays during Trump’s first term in office gave Dominion an opportunity to redesign the project with next-generation wind turbines. Those delays also enabled Dominion to take advantage of a new generation of turbine installation vessels that are purpose-built to cut offshore construction costs.

The results speak for themselves. In its October 30 report, Dominion indicated that CVOW costs were still consistent with its capital budget, even accounting for the cost of last year’s stop-work order and costs related to Trump’s tariff wars.

“The estimates on the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) also continue to fall,” Maritime Executive summarized. “After starting with a forecasted range of $80-$90 per MWh, and adjustments for changes after the change in administrations, they have lowered the LCOE to $62, down from an estimate of $83 presented in August” (LCOE is a calculation that provides a common ground for comparing costs among different forms of power generation).

Maritime Executive further reported that Dominion expects to save its ratepayers about $5 billion on fuel over the first 10 years of operation.

Trump’s war on wind has also petered out elsewhere. The Revolution Wind project off the coasts of Connecticut and Massachusetts has also been a target of  multiple stop-work orders over the past two years, with the latest hammer coming down just two weeks ago, when the 704-megawatt wind farm was almost complete.

Revolution Wind is now fully operational, joining the nearby Vineyard Wind project which also endured multiple attacks from Trump. As reported by public radio station WBUR, the savings from Revolution Wind is expected to ripple out through New England, saving $500 million for ratepayers in the region every year.

As for the domestic offshore wind industry writ large, the US lost thousands of onshore supply chain jobs all around the US in addition to job losses related to portside and offshore operation. However, the trade organization Oceantic Network is already prepping for a comeback. “The road to recovery for the embattled American offshore wind industry starts today with a new political mandate to tackle the affordability crisis,” Oceantic President and CEO Liz said in a public statement celebrating the Republican Party’s crushing defeat in the 202y midterm elections.

#5787. Booze, Tobacco Together in Pregnancy May Worsen Baby's Facial Abnormalities

— Smaller face size, reduced growth, and dysmorphism worse with combined exposure, study shows

Prenatal exposure to both alcohol and tobacco smoke impacted the baby's facial development more than either alone, a longitudinal study from South Africa showed.

Three-dimensional facial scans at 1 month and 1 year of age showed the greatest differences in facial shape, size, and growth with co-exposure from early pregnancy compared with none or single-substance exposure, Michael Suttie, PhD, of the University of Oxford in England, and colleagues reported in Pediatrics.

For girls, tobacco plus alcohol exposure was associated with greater reductions in facial growth and measurements around the eyes. Craniofacial growth didn't catch up by age 1 for girls exposed continuously to both substances in utero. For boys, dual prenatal exposure was linked to reduced nasal growth, resulting in smaller noses at 1 year.

"Findings highlight tobacco's potentiating effect on alcohol-related craniofacial harm," the researchers wrote. "These findings highlight the importance of interventions targeting alcohol and smoking cessation during pregnancy to reduce teratogenic risk."

An estimated 5.4% of U.S. women smoke during pregnancy, which carries known risk of craniofacial developmental issues for the baby, including craniosynostosis and orofacial clefts. Some 9.8% of pregnant women globally consume alcohol, which can lead to the baby having facial characteristics such as nasal shortening, midline differences, midfacial hypoplasia, ocular differences, and mandibular anomalies aside from some of the most identifiable signs of fetal alcohol syndrome: a smooth philtrum above a short upper lip and shortened width from the inner to outer corner of the eye.

"Both teratogens are known to disrupt neural crest cell migration, survival, and differentiation, processes essential for the formation of midline facial structures, ocular features, and nasal morphology," the researchers noted. "Nicotine exposure potentially compounds this disruption [by alcohol] through oxidative stress, hypoxia, and nicotine-induced vasoconstriction, which may impair oxygen and nutrient delivery during critical periods of facial morphogenesis."

To look for evidence that the impact of these substances might be additive, Suttie's group examined the Safe Passage Study, a prospective cohort of more than 7,000 pregnancies in low socioeconomic communities in Cape Town, South Africa, which has one of the world's highest rates of alcohol use in pregnancy. The cohort largely comprised women of mixed ancestry, known as South African Colored.

Of the more than 7,000 participants in the study, the analysis homed in on the subset of 634 participants who had 3D facial imaging of their infants at age 1 month and 1 year and antenatal substance exposure data. Exclusion criteria included illicit drug use by the mother (including marijuana) and genetic diagnoses in infants.

Alcohol and smoking exposures had been assessed via interview at each prenatal visit, with frequency and quantity both captured. Continuous exposure was defined as exposure in the first trimester and any subsequent trimester. There were 152 infants categorized as without exposure, 48 with continuous alcohol-only exposure, 149 with continuous smoking-only exposure, 150 with continuous co-exposure, and 135 with continuous smoking and any alcohol use.

Continuous prenatal co-exposure to smoking and alcohol was associated with reduced facial size compared with both controls and single-exposure groups (P<0.05), driven by differences among girls. The single-exposure groups showed no differences compared with controls.

"Our findings of sex-specific dysmorphism are consistent with prior work suggesting differential vulnerability to prenatal alcohol exposure by sex," Suttie and colleagues noted.

Continuous co-exposure was associated with greater facial dysmorphism overall, with the biggest difference at 1 month (P<0.001) but still significant at 1 year (P<0.05). Consistent midline displacement was seen with co-exposure at both time points. More outward lateral movement of the inner canthi of the eye was also seen with co-exposure at both time points (P<0.05).

Limitations included the need to scan infants while sleeping, potential modification by maternal nutritional deficiencies, and unknown generalizability to populations with different genetic profiles.

"Our results contribute to a growing body of evidence on the harms of co-exposures, and we encourage clinicians and healthcare authorities to emphasize the potential harm of concurrent smoking and alcohol use during pregnancy," the researchers concluded.

#5786. Rivian Doesn't Have Dealerships, So How Do You Test Drive One?

Running a business isn't easy. Aside from keeping on top of nagging accountants and office politics, you need to think about profitability and even sustainability these days – the latter two are particularly important if you're an automaker. The pivot toward electrification hasn't just been an opportunity for brands to re-establish themselves, but also for them to rethink how they run their business. Rivian is an excellent example.

The California-based marque is now well established thanks to vehicles like the R1S and the R2, which is even better than you'd hoped, and it's done so without having a single physical dealership around. Instead, it has various Spaces across the United States in places like Chicago, Denver, and New York. Interested customers can visit one of these Spaces to get a feel for Rivian's products in person before they order one through an online-only process. If you're looking to test-drive a Rivian before committing, this can also be done at many of the Spaces and Service + Demo Centers.

First, there are a few boxes you need to check before you can drive a Rivian. You'll need to be at least 21 years of age and hold a valid driver's license. Depending on the length and specific purpose of the drive, you might also need to bring proof of vehicle insurance. If applicable, you'll also need to bring and install your own car seat for any passengers younger than eight. Finally, you'll have to sign a liability waiver on-site before driving.

Okay, got all that checked? Good. Now you're ready to book the time and place of your test drive using the Rivian website. Your first decision is to pick which model you want to drive, and that includes the R1S – one of only two large SUVs with a 2026 IIHS Top Safety Pick+ award. Then you'll need to pick which location you'll visit and when, before submitting your key details (contact information, preferred popcorn flavor, you know the drill).

When you arrive at the Space — and we have no doubt you'll be punctual and fittingly dressed — you'll need to check in with one of the Rivian specialists. Expect a quick walkaround of your requested test car model after that, to get you up to speed on the car's features and key information. They probably won't tell you how many liters of popcorn the trunk can hold, though, so that may be worth asking.

With all the formalities taken care of, a Rivian specialist will accompany you on your test drive, which is said to typically last around 30 minutes and take place on public roads. If you thought it was going to be an off-road thrash to prove you have what it takes to race in the Dakar, sorry to burst your bubble. At certain locations, Rivian offers an extended demo drive for up to 24 hours. And no, that's not a ticket to race at Le Mans either.

Once your drive is wrapped up, you'll probably be asked the all-important question before being on your way. It's as simple as that.

#5784. Buc-Ee's CEO Said He Didn't Want To Operate In Blue States, And Now There's Stores In At Least Five More

I had the pleasure of experiencing Buc-ee's Beaver Nuggets for the first time on a recent road trip. It's an experience I'll get to repeat soon as the popular chain of ginormous gas stations and convenience stores expands into my adopted home state of Arkansas, among other places. It'll be interesting to see if the midterm election results affect those expansion plans, as Buc-ee's president and co-founder Arch "Beaver" Aplin III has expressed a desire to avoid blue states, according to Fox Business.

At the grand opening of a new location in Benton, Arkansas, Aplin said:

"I'm starting to realize life's too short to try to build in places that people don't appreciate what you're bringing, versus a place like this where people do appreciate what you are building," he said.

Conservative states typically promote business-friendly and family-oriented policies that align with Buc-ee's values, Aplin said.

"That leadership, that concept, that idea of conservative, business-friendly, family-oriented concept works so much better if it trickles down from the very leadership from the top at the governor's office, at the congressman, at senator, at the mayor, the representatives," he said.

The thing is, Aplin no longer has that choice. The blue tsunami of the midterm election has turned several states formerly controlled by Republicans over to the Democrats at many of those levels, and in some cases all of them.

Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time 🤷‍♂️

The most notable upset from the election is right in Buc-ee's home state of Texas. President Trump hand-picked the scandal-ridden Ken Paxton to run against Democratic contender James Talarico for U.S. Senate, pushing out incumbent Republican John Cornyn during the primaries (maybe he won't be able to steal the Space Shuttle after all). Elon Musk invested more than $200 million backing Paxton's election campaign. Despite all that, Talarico won, making him the first Democratic Senator from Texas since 1993. Ted Cruz remains in the Senate, but possibly only because he wasn't up for re-election this year.

It's not just the Senate, either. Governor Greg Abbott lost re-election to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, and the Texas House gained a slight Democratic majority as well. Buc-ee's now finds itself deeply entrenched and headquartered in a blue state, as unlikely as it was for Texas to flip like this. If Buc-ee's really doesn't want to do business in blue states, it's going to have to find a new home. So will Elon Musk, for that matter, just five years after fleeing California for the same reason.

Where else could Buc-ee's move? Some states remain solidly Republican, such as Alabama, Florida, Kentucky, and Tennessee, and would likely welcome Buc-ee's "business-friendly and family-oriented values." Missouri remained red, though Democrat Fred Wellman flipped a House seat held by incumbent Ann Wagner.

In Arkansas, where Aplin made his comments back in August, Senator Tom Cotton, who encourages using your car as a weapon, remains in office. Opponent Hallie Shoffner ran a strong race based on the issues farmers are facing rather than the Trump Administration's culture wars. Even in crimson red Arkansas, every single county shifted more toward Democrats than in the 2024 presidential election, according to the Associated Press.

Other states besides Texas flipped from Republican to Democrat as well. In Arizona, Democrats will hold the state house, senate, and governor for the first time in 60 years. The Colorado House flipped from a 50/50 split to seven of eight seats going to Democrats. In Ohio, Amy Acton beat DOGE conspirator Vivek Ramaswamy for governor despite (or perhaps because of) a last-minute attack campaign against Acton featuring her estranged mother. The state house flipped Democrat, and Sherrod Brown ousted incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted.

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms will be not only the first Black woman elected governor of Georgia, but of any U.S. state ever. Similarly, the Mississippi Senate race (at the time of writing) remains too close to call, because Scott Colom holds a 0.1% lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. If Colom wins, he'll be the first Democrat Senator for Mississippi in 40 years, and the state's first Black Senator since Hiram R. Revels, who became the country's first Black Senator ever in 1870.

We'll have to wait and see whether this big blue tsunami has any effects on Buc-ee's expansion plans, as well as plans in states where it currently exists. Our own Brad Brownell called it the sickness at the heart of America, yet even he can't stop himself from loving it. And while I wouldn't call myself a beaver believer, I may have to take a motorcycle ride over to Benton for some barbecue and more Beaver Nuggets.

#5782. Are These 9 Concepts And Sporty Coupés Pre-Ford Mustang Pony Cars?

History books love romantic tales, like the one where Lee Iacocca, father of the Mustang, was responsible for giving birth to a whole new category of vehicles: pony cars. Sure, he was behind the creation of the most popular such vehicle, but the pony car concept was in the brewing stage years before the first-gen Mustang Mk1. While not strictly pony cars, these concepts and production sporty coupés already flirted with the concept of an enthusiast-grade compact car.

Of course, we don't mean to diminish Iacocca's genius. Yes, he didn't invent the wheel, but he definitely read the room better than his counterparts. In fact, some of the cars featured in this piece influenced him to create the special team of engineers that worked on the Mustang. From early Ford-based compact sports cars like the Budd XT-Bird Concept and Ford Falcon Futura Sport to rear-engine fun machines like the Chevrolet Corvair Monza Turbo, these pre-Mustang models warmed the public to the pony car idea.

Iacocca wasn't the first to toy with the idea of a compact sports car for the masses. Edward Gowan Budd, one of the early 20th century's most important engineers and entrepreneurs, already had dabbled with the idea of a 2+2 sports car for the masses. Better yet, he pitched a working prototype of the XT-Bird directly to Iacocca, likely planting the pony-car seed in his mind.

The proposed car was based on a 1961 Ford Falcon unibody and a modified body shell from a 1955 to 1957 Ford Thunderbird. This let Budd's company, Budd-American Motors, stretch the Thunderbird's 102-inch wheelbase by 7.5 inches, turning it from a two-seater into a 2+2. Yes, the rear seats were tight and mostly unusable, but the 2+2 configuration became a hallmark of pony cars, allowing buyers to take their friends and family on a joyride.

Speaking of which, the XT-Bird Concept was equipped with a 170-cubic-inch (2.8-liter) inline-6 engine. Yes, it's not a V8, but Budd boosted it with a supercharger, so it should've been potent enough for the time. Power figures were never disclosed, but we know the XT-Bird Concept had a three-speed manual.

While the XT-Bird Concept influenced Ford in developing the Mustang, its clumsy attempt to modernize the classic Thunderbird fell flat. Budd smoothed out the Thunderbird's rear fins and accentuated headlight housings, resulting in a bland, somewhat forgettable design.

Ford never accepted Budd's XT-Bird proposal, but that didn't stop the ambitious engineer from making another attempt at an early pony car. Unveiled mere months later, the XR-400 Concept was another fully functional, production-ready sporty convertible.

This time, though, Budd used a Rambler Ambassador chassis and proposed the idea to American Motors Corporation. He went so far to create a full development plan, estimating a low $4.1 million to bring the car to market. Because the XR-400 Concept utilized an existing AMC platform, tooling and production would've also been cheaper than building the car from the ground up. Had AMC greenlit the XR-400, it would've beaten both the Barracuda and the Mustang to showroom floors, completely rewriting pony car history. Heck, it might even have saved AMC from the Chrysler buyout. Instead, AMC surrendered its head start and played catch-up with the other old-school pony cars using the 1968 Javelin.

Was the XR-400 good enough to save AMC, though? Well, it certainly looked sportier than the XT-Bird Concept, while also bringing AMC's 327-cubic-inch (5.36-liter) V8 into the fray. Budd even mounted the engine lower in the chassis, just as you'd expect in a sports car; shortened Ambassador's floor pan by 14.3 inches; and moved the cabin back 16.24 inches to give the car sportier proportions. The XR-400 Concept still offered 2+2 seating, though with less space in the rear than a Ford Mustang. Still, the XR-400 Concept was a textbook pony car convertible, two full years before the press coined the term.

Budd wasn't alone in developing a compact sports car for the masses. Ford concurrently worked on a mid-engine Mustang concept that could've completely changed the nameplate's trajectory. With a sharp, wedge-like design, pop-up headlights, two-seat cabin layout, and a tight 90-inch wheelbase, the Mustang I Concept served as the antithesis of Ford's lineup at the time: the Falcon, Fairlane, Galaxie, and Thunderbird.

The Mustang I was one of those cool Ford concepts that never made it to production, but it spearheaded the development of America's most popular pony car. Crucially, it was a fully functioning sports car. Yes, it only had a 1.5-liter V4 engine making up to 100 hp (gross) in race trim, but it was also featherlight at only 1,544 pounds. This race-car-level lightness was achieved by using an advanced space-frame chassis and aluminum body panels. As a result, the Mustang I Concept reached 115 mph, an impressive figure for such a tiny motor. And, sure, the engine was only a half-V8, but at least it revved to relatively high 7,500 rpm.

Handling was a big reason why Ford toyed with a mid-engine layout for the Mustang. Unlike later pony cars, the Mustang I Concept felt stable and balanced in the corners. It stayed flat during cornering, too, perhaps thanks to the integrated roll bar that strengthened the chassis. Ford was so convinced of the concept's abilities that it organized a publicity stunt at the United States Grand Prix at what was then known as the Watkins Glen Raceway, in Watkins Glen, New York. With star F1 driver Dan Gurney behind the wheel, the Mustang I Concept lapped the circuit almost as fast as an F1 car of the day.

While the Mustang I Concept introduced the famous horse emblem, it was the Mustang II Concept that was the real preview of the production car. Featuring a classic pony car shape with a long hood, relatively short rear deck, chopped roofline, and tri-bar taillights, it looked similar to the Mustang Mk1. It was 5 inches longer than the production car, which gave it a somewhat sleeker look, but the Mustang blueprint is definitely there.

The similarities weren't only skin deep. Like the production car, the Mustang II Concept was also built over a Ford Falcon unibody chassis, and had the right power train — a 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) high-performance V8 with a four-speed manual transmission. Like the first Mustang concept, this was also a convertible, albeit with a removable fiberglass hard top. In classic pony car fashion, the Mustang II Concept offered 2+2 seating inside. Being a concept car, it also previewed some tech-forward features, like an electric trunk release.

Much like its mid-engine predecessor, the Mustang II Concept was dressed in stark white with blue center stripes, and was also shown at Watkins Glen. This time, though, Ford passed the opportunity to show its abilities on the track. Still, Ford made sure the audience could clearly hear the V8 rumble by filling the valve lifters with wax, which apparently gave the engine a race-car-like big-cam note.

The Corvair was Chevy's revolutionary compact car designed to compete with the Volkswagen Beetle, featuring a rear-mounted, air-cooled flat-6 engine, multiple body styles, and a spacious interior. It proved to be an ill-fated attempt, but it also gave us one of the most interesting 1960s sports cars — the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo.

The car that introduced turbocharging to the masses was the Mustang's opposite, given the Mustang's front-mounted, water-cooled V8. But it forced Lee Iacocca into creating the "Fairlane Committee" — the secret group of executives and engineers that decided Ford needed an attractive sports car, despite leading compact-car sales with the Falcon. And it was the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo that served as the committee's inspiration, at least in terms of character and market positioning.

Of course, the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo wasn't a pony car, per se. You could even argue that it's closer to the Porsche 911 Turbo, which arrived 11 years later with a turbocharged, air-cooled flat-6 in the back. Still, it was an enthusiast car with four seats, same as every pony car. The 2.4-liter turbocharged flat-6 also produced a healthy 150 hp, enough for a 0-60 sprint in 10.3 seconds, though, unsurprisingly, it suffered from significant turbo lag. For 1965, Chevrolet introduced the upgraded Corvair Corsa, which packed a larger 2.7-liter engine with 180 hp and accelerated to 60 in 7.8 seconds.

The Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo was also equipped with some enthusiast-grade features, like a standard four-speed manual; instrument panel with multiple gauges, including a tachometer; and bucket seats.

Strip away the attractive body style, and the 1964½ Mustang is essentially a Ford Falcon Futura. Launched as a direct answer to the Corvair Monza, the Falcon Futura, particularly in the Sprint trim, gave customers a taste of what the future of Ford sports cars hold.

The Futura Sport/Sprint shared most mechanical parts with the Mustang, and was even equipped with Ford's 164-horsepower, 260-cubic-inch (4.3-liter) Challenger V8 and a four-speed manual transmission. Yes, that's a far cry from the most powerful editions of the Mustang, like the 306-horsepower GT350, but good enough to serve as a stopgap model before Futura's more popular brethren arrived on the scene. Since the Futura was relatively light at 3,011 pounds, the V8 also propelled it to 60 in a solid 9.5 seconds.

To show its intention of attracting enthusiast drivers, Ford gave the Falcon Futura Sprint heavy-duty suspension and equipped it with a tachometer, bucket seats, and sporty steering wheel. Buyers could get the V8 as an option with all other trims, too, but would miss out on these features.

Despite having all the pony car features, minus the sporty styling, the Falcon Futura remained a low-volume proposition. Ford sold 15,081 during the first year of production, of which 10,479 two-door hardtops and 4,602 convertibles. Ford kept the Futura Sprint in production through 1965, but with the Mustang already in full swing by then, sales dwindled quickly. In fact, Ford sold 11 Mustangs to every Falcon, despite the Mustang being more expensive.

Studebaker might not be the first automaker you'd associate with pony cars. Still, it created one of the ultimate pre-pony sleepers with the Lark Daytona. From its compact dimensions to the highly potent engine in its R1 and R2 models, the Lark Daytona had all the ingredients for being called a pony car.

Based on the compact Lark, the sporty coupé Daytona version had pillarless doors and an unusual upright design. In that sense, it didn't look much like the "official" pony cars, but under its unassuming design, it hid a 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) V8. The engine was available in naturally aspirated (R1) and supercharged form (R2).

With 240 horsepower on tap, the non-boosted motor was already powerful enough to usurp rivals like the Corvair Monza Spyder Turbo and Falcon Futura, sprinting to 60 in the 7-second range when paired with the optional four-speed manual. Meanwhile, the supercharged version produced 289 hp, enough for a quicker 0-60 time of less than 7 seconds with the four-speed manual. The Lark Daytona was also available with automatic and manual three-speeds and a smaller 2.8-liter six-cylinder engine.

In many ways, the Lark Daytona punched way above its class, especially during the pre-pony-car era. Studebaker, though, couldn't outrun its misfortunes (our deep dive into Studebaker's rise and fall explains its desire for glory). The automaker was flying so high, in 1963 it launched a Corvette competitor called the Avanti. This sleek sports car was based on the Lark, but thanks to its more aerodynamic body, it reached a top speed of 178.5 mph using a 335-hp tune of Studebaker's supercharged V8.

The Valiant was crucial for Plymouth. It brought the brand back to life after dismal 1962 sales, and its sporty version, the Signet 200, served as the backbone for the world's first pony car, the 1964 Barracuda. Since the Valiant and Barracuda shared most of their mechanicals, it wouldn't be wrong to say the Signet was also a pre-Ford Mustang pony car. The blueprint was already there. The Valiant Signet 200 was a two-door hardtop coupé or convertible aimed at enthusiasts, equipped with front vinyl bucket seats, chrome accents, and from 1964 on, an optional 273-cubic-inch (4.5-liter) V8.

Initially, the V8 engine produced 180 hp, but for 1965, Plymouth increased the compression ratio and replaced the two-barrel BBD carburetor with a four-barrel one, boosting it to 235 hp. That engine could also be paired with an optional Hurst four-speed manual, though most models were equipped with three-speed manual/automatic transmissions.

The entry-level engine was a 170-cubic-inch (2.8 liter) Slant-Six, though, good for only 101 hp. Still, to showcase the car's sporty pretensions, Plymouth also offered a lighter all-aluminum 225-cubic-inch (3.7-liter) Slant-Six with 145 hp initially, but it was quickly replaced with a cast-iron version because of poor reliability. The Valiant Signet 200 was never available with disc brakes or heavy-duty suspension, upgrades that started being offered as options once the real pony cars took over.

Dodge also had a sort of an early pony car that shared the A-body platform with the Valiant. However, the Dart was noticeably less compact, stretching roughly 10 inches longer, which also increased its weight. Still, like its sibling, the Dart was available with the 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six and 273-cubic-inch V8 engines.

The Mustang might be the most influential, but the 1964 Plymouth Barracuda beat it to the punch by only 16 days, becoming the world's first pony car. Still, it wasn't a brand-new model, but a fastback body style of the Valiant Signet 200. See, the Barracuda didn't only share its platform and engines with Plymouth's compact car, but also carried Valiant badges on the body. Still, it was significantly more attractive, with a unique wraparound rear glass giving it a more dynamic, sporty look.

As far as performance goes, though, there was nothing to differentiate the two models. Like the Valiant Signet 200, the Barracuda was available with the 170-cubic-inch and 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six engines, alongside the 273-cubic-inch V8 with up to 235 hp in the Commando model. Enthusiast buyers could choose a Hurst four-speed manual with the V8, with Chrysler's three-speed auto also available.

Yes, the Valiant Signet 200 had exactly the same engine and transmission options, but from 1965, the Barracuda also had the supporting equipment of a true pony car. As part of the Formula S package, the Barracuda received an upgraded suspension and wider tires for sharper handling, with a tachometer inside.

These improvements let the Barracuda compete more closely with the Mustang, though Ford's legend was the better-rounded proposition. The Mustang was available with a more potent, 289-cubic-inch (4.7-liter) V8 with up to 271 hp, disc brakes, and a more comprehensive handling package with upgraded shocks, springs, and stabilizer bars.

#5781. America’s New Shipbuilding Orders Are Expensive Bets on Fossil Freight

South Korea’s Hanwha Group owns the Philadelphia shipyard that has become a centerpiece of Washington’s attempt to rebuild American commercial shipbuilding. Its Hanwha Ocean and Hanwha Systems subsidiaries acquired the US yard in December 2024. The investment creates and sustains American production capacity and jobs while transferring shipbuilding expertise, technology and training from South Korea to US workers. The facility is in America, but its corporate ownership remains South Korean. The company’s published orderbook, however, tells a more complicated story: two liquefied natural gas carriers, four firm orders for oil and chemical tankers, and options for another six tankers. Three LNG-fueled container ships ordered by Matson in 2022 predate the current administration. The newer LNG and tanker orders come from Hanwha’s own shipping affiliates. They can help restart production, but buying ships from another company in the same group does not demonstrate that independent shipowners will pay US construction prices.

The price gap is difficult to dismiss. Kinder Morgan’s January 2026 investor presentation estimates that a new medium-range Jones Act tanker would cost more than $240 million and require a long-term charter above $115,000 per day to justify construction. The existing charter market was around $90,000 per day. Kinder Morgan operates 16 tankers, with its fleet fully utilized, yet the gap between current charter revenue and the cost of a replacement vessel remains substantial. High utilization establishes a need for shipping services; it does not establish a financeable order for a new American-built tanker at today’s prices.

Coastal petroleum shipping also competes with other domestic infrastructure. A 2025 report to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission estimated moving gasoline from Houston to New York Harbor at under 8 cents per gallon by pipeline, about 20 cents by ship, and roughly 35 cents by rail. These illustrative route costs do not cover every destination, and tankers remain essential where pipelines are unavailable. They do show why expensive new tankers cannot count on charter customers accepting whatever price domestic construction requires. Longer term, the International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles displaced 1.7 million barrels of oil per day worldwide in 2025 and could displace about 5 million by 2030 under its policy scenarios. That does not mean US tanker demand vanishes, but fleet investment must account for changes in the cargo market over several decades.

LNG export carriers have a more plausible near-term growth market, although their prospects are different from the prospects of LNG-fueled container ships. US gas exports may expand, and LNG tankers will be needed to carry them. The commercial test for a US-built LNG carrier is whether it can win an arm’s-length contract against established Korean, Japanese and Chinese shipyards. Hanwha’s plan to train Philadelphia workers through its Korean shipyards can strengthen US industrial capability, and affiliated orders can provide an initial production run. The central uncertainty is whether independent buyers will still choose these ships once the group’s internal demand and any cargo preference are removed.

A broader domestic vessel market already exists. US-flag Great Lakes freighters carried 71.3 million tons in 2025, much of it iron ore, limestone, cement, coal and other bulk materials. Those cargo flows will change as steelmaking and energy systems evolve, while ferry services, harbour vessels, inland cargo craft and multipurpose ships will still require renewal. Battery-electric and hybrid-electric propulsion offer practical options on routes with manageable energy requirements and reliable charging access. Large, long-distance bulk ships need a more selective technology assessment, rather than an assumption that every vessel can run on batteries.

Recent projects demonstrate what a committed customer can contribute to ship economics. CMA CGM, Nike and Gemadept launched an electric inland barge in Vietnam for a 180-kilometre round trip. Nike agreed to fill 90% of its capacity for eight years, helping justify a vessel reportedly costing about twice as much as its diesel equivalent. A dedicated charging installation and renewable electricity form part of the service. That is a commercially structured freight proposition, with its higher capital cost supported by contracted utilization and expected operating savings.

Electric propulsion does not cure the American shipbuilding cost problem by itself. Washington State’s three new hybrid-electric ferries carry a $714.5 million shipbuilding contract, and the state’s estimate including additional equipment and other program expenses is approximately $1.15 billion. Construction has started; the ferries are not yet in service. The path to a productive shipbuilding industry still runs through standardized designs, modular fabrication, trained workers, repeat orders, reliable delivery and falling labor-hours per vessel. It would be a mistake to treat electrification as a substitute for manufacturing reform.

Hanwha’s South Korean capital and know-how could contribute to that reform by developing US suppliers and production skills that serve several vessel classes. That is a meaningful way to rebuild domestic capability even though the parent company remains foreign-owned. Its progress should ultimately be measured by independent repeat customers, improving construction costs and commercially competitive vessels, rather than affiliated orders or investment announcements. A US maritime strategy anchored to the fossil-fuel cargoes of today risks missing a growing opportunity to build modern domestic vessels for the freight, port and ferry services of tomorrow.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Hanwha’s orders, Kinder Morgan’s tanker economics and the market for repeatable electric and hybrid maritime construction. It follows my earlier analysis of the Jones Act’s shipbuilding capacity gap.

#5780. Solar carport project at California medical plaza solves tricky energy billing

Watthub Renewables and Sunrock Distributed Generation completed a 322-kW solar photovoltaic system at Irvine Heritage Medical Plaza, the three-story Class A medical office building in Irvine, California. Solar modules were installed to carports covering approximately 108 parking spots, turning bare asphalt into shaded, covered parking and into the building’s primary source of electricity.

Watthub Renewables, Sunrock Distributed Generation and SunRenu Solar completed a 322-kW carport solar project at Irvine Heritage Medical plaza in Irvine, California. Credit: Watthub Renewables

The system is expected to generate approximately 515,690 kWh in its first year, covering the majority of the plaza’s annual electricity consumption. It was delivered under a 25-year power purchase agreement requiring no upfront capital from Irvine Heritage’s ownership. Watthub and Sunrock DG financed, engineered and contracted by SunRenu Solar. Sunrock DG now owns and maintains the array, while the property buys the power it produces at a rate below Southern California Edison’s.

Irvine Heritage Medical Plaza was built in 2008 on just over two acres, with approximately 40,000 sq ft of medical suite.

“Medical office is one of the few property types where the parking lot is part of the patient experience,” said Aaron Moston, director at Watthub Renewables. “Somebody’s coming out of a medical or dental procedure at two in the afternoon in August. Whether their car is 140 degrees or 95 degrees is not a small thing. Carports were the right structure here before we ever ran the production model — the fact that they also happen to be the best south-facing real estate on the property is what made the project work.”

Irvine Heritage Medical Plaza is master metered, meaning the entire building draws electricity through a single Southern California Edison (SCE) account on the GS-3-TOU commercial rate, and that cost flows through to tenants inside their charges rather than through individual utility bills. For years, that meant every practice in the building carried a share of an electric bill it could not see or control in a utiliyt territory with rate increases and, during the summer, on-peak energy.

Since solar generation is netted at the master meter, the savings are not captured by one tenant — they reduce the building’s total electricity cost.

“A master meter is usually described as a disadvantage — tenants have no visibility into their usage and the owner absorbs every swing in the energy bill,” said Wilson Chang, CEO at Sunrock DG. “For a solar project it’s the opposite. One meter, one interconnection, one bill to offset and every suite in the building benefits automatically. It’s the simplest way to bring solar to a multi-tenant property.”

Earlier this year, developed another 300-kW solar carport project for the Foothill Medical Association in Foothill, California. The system was also commissioned with a PPA.

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5779. 5 Prestigious International Car Shows Where Automakers Reveal New Models

Changing industry dynamics and the rise of livestreaming have led many physical conventions and events to either go away entirely (most notably the Geneva Motor Show and the E3 video game expo) or shift to digital formats (Apple's major product keynotes). Thankfully, a lot of traditional car shows have stuck around globally and remain among the most important entries on the calendar for automakers.

Setting up a pavilion at an auto show, especially a reputable and longstanding one, can be expensive, but it gives automakers a global platform to unveil brand-new production cars, showcase wild concepts and designs, and introduce new technologies to journalists, industry executives, and prospective buyers. It's also always fun to walk through the pavilions at a motor show and check out new cars up close and in the flesh.

While hundreds of automotive exhibitions and trade shows are held across the world every year, there's an upper echelon of car shows for which automakers save their best reveals. These include long-running motor shows like IAA Mobility, exhibitions of growing significance like Auto China and Auto Shanghai, and Monterey Car Week, which isn't a convention but a week-long series of prestigious automotive events.

The Paris Motor Show, also known as Mondial de l'Auto, is one of the world's oldest automotive conventions, dating all the way back to 1898. Held biennially in the French capital, the Paris Motor Show has historically been a major platform for the country's top domestic automakers — Renault, Peugeot, Citroen, and the like — to reveal their latest and greatest to the world.

These include the Peugeot 402 in 1935 (one of the first European cars to feature a curvy, streamlined design), the Renault 4CV in 1946 and Citroen 2CV in 1948 (both instrumental in bringing personal mobility to a post-World War II, cash-strapped France), the Renault 5 Turbo in 1978 (a raucous 160-hp mid-engined supermini), and more. Landmark introductions from non-French automakers include the Lamborghini Sesto Elemento in 2010 and the Ferrari 250 Europa GT in 1954, along with the Porsche Carrera GT concept and Koenigsegg CC8S in 2000.

The 2026 iteration of the Paris Motor Show was held in October, and prominently featured concept cars like an all-electric revival of the Citroen 2CV, the striking Alfa Romeo Cuorerosso, the Peugeot E-T16 and RCZ Vision, the Alpine A310 Vision, the Renault E-Space, and the Fiat Multiplay.

Germany's International Motor Show or Internationale Automobil-Ausstellung, now branded IAA Mobility, beats the Paris Motor Show by just one year to claim the title of the oldest surviving car show in the world. Throughout its 129-year history, the biennial event has been held in various German cities, including Frankfurt am Main, Berlin, Leipzig, Cologne, and Munich. In a similar vein to the Paris Motor Show, IAA Mobility serves as a major showcase for Germany's big automakers, like BMW, Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, and Porsche.

Notable debuts at the IAA throughout history include the BMW 1500 in 1961 (it introduced the brand-saving Neue Klasse lineup), a concept version of the Volkswagen Golf GTI in 1975 (widely considered the forefather of hot hatchbacks), the Mercedes-Benz 190E 2.3-16 in 1983 (the record-breaking pioneer of sporty compact luxury sedans), the Audi RS6 Avant in 2007 (a super-cool V10-powered wagon), the Porsche 918 Spyder in 2013 (part of the holy trinity of hybrid hypercars), and many more.

The IAA Mobility held in 2025featured the motor-show debuts of the BMW iX3, the electric Mercedes-Benz GLC and Concept AMG GT XX, the Audi Concept C, the Porsche 911 Turbo S (992.2), and a near-production version of the all-electric Volkswagen ID. Polo supermini.

Held since 1954 and currently a biennial event, the Japan Mobility Show (formerly the Tokyo Motor Show) has cemented itself as a major venue for, you guessed it, Japanese automakers to showcase new cars, concepts, and experimental technologies. Toyota, Honda, Mazda, and Nissan particularly have been prominent participants at the Japan Mobility Show throughout its history.

The Japan Mobility Show has played host to the reveals of iconic cars like the Mazda Cosmo Sport in 1963 (the world's first mass-produced sports car to be powered by a two-rotor rotary engine), the Toyota 2000GT in 1965 (one of Japan's strongest rivals to European performance cars), the Nissan Skyline GT-R in 1968 (we're all familiar with this one, aren't we?), a concept version of the Toyota Prius in 1995 (the world's first mass-produced hybrid passenger car), and the Lexus LFA in 2009 (arguably the most sensational supercar from Japan).

At the 202 Japan Mobility Show we saw the reveal of the rakish-looking next-gen Toyota Corolla concept, along with other concept cars and prototypes like the Century Coupe, the Honda 0 Alpha, the wild six-wheeled Lexus LS luxury van, and more.

China holds not one, but two major global motor shows: Auto Shanghai and the Beijing International Automotive Exhibition (also known as Auto China or the Beijing Motor Show). These events are held in alternating years (Beijing in even-numbered years, Shanghai in odd-numbered years), which means there's a big car show in China on an annual basis. Since China is the world's largest automotive market by a huge margin, and a wellspring of innovation for new-energy vehicles (EVs and plug-in hybrids), Auto Shanghai and Beijing Motor Show are highly important platforms for Chinese and global automakers alike.

Chinese automakers like BYD, Dongfeng, and Hongqi have debuted some pretty wild stuff at Auto Shanghai and the Beijing Motor Show. Specifically, BYD showcased the Yangwang U8 (a full-size luxury off-roader that can perform a 360-degree tank turn and float on water for up to 30 minutes) and the Yangwang U9 (a 1,200-plus hp electric supercar that can jump short distances and drive on three wheels) in 2023. Hongqi debuted the Guoya limousine in 2025 as China's answer to established full-size European luxury sedans, while Dongfeng debuted the MHERO M-Hunter concept in 2024 — a bonkers-looking electric off-roader with a full carbon-fiber body and over 14,750 lb-ft of wheel-side torque.

As for the global carmakers that we're more familiar with, Mercedes-Benz pulled the covers off the electric G-Class at the Beijing Motor Show in 2024. At the same event, Lamborghini unveiled the Urus SE as the Italian marque's first hybrid SUV, and Mini revealed the Aceman as its first electric-only offering.

Unlike the conventional motor shows discussed above, California's Monterey Car Week is a series of automotive events centered on luxury, performance, and collector cars — both modern and old-school. Held across the Monterey Peninsula every August and tracing its roots to the first Pebble Beach Concours in 1950, Monterey Car Week is a must-attend event for any gearhead in the U.S., thanks to renowned and prestigious attractions like The Quail, A Motorsports Gathering; Exotics on Broadway; and the Pebble Beach Concours d'Elegance.

Automakers show up to Monterey Car Week to reveal exciting production cars, limited-run specials, and concepts. Bugatti has debuted one-offs and few-offs like the Destrier, Centodieci, and Brouillard during Monterey Car Week. American hypercar maker Hennessey showcased the Venom F5 Roadster in 2022 and the Blackbird in 2026, while McLaren also unveiled the McL 6GT concept this year to preview a forthcoming new model from the British brand.

In addition to exhibiting exotic machines, Monterey Car Week hosts auctions from houses like RM Sotheby's, and some of these are very high-profile — to the tune of tens of millions of dollars. The most expensive car sold at this year's Monterey Car Week was a 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe, which went for the princely sum of $42.9 million. Also, a "Tailor Made" Ferrari Luce fetched a handsome $40 million, with the proceeds funneled entirely to charity. On the other end of the price spectrum, great cars often sell for under $10,000 every year at Monterey Car Week.

#5778. Hormone Therapy and Cancer Risk; Oncology Pay Cut; Mammograms Post-Double Mastectomy

— News, features, and commentary about cancer-related issues.

Doctors are warning not to overlook the small increase in breast cancer risk associated with certain hormonal therapies for treating menopause symptoms. (New York Times)

In related news, the FDA removed boxed warnings about breast cancer, cardiovascular disease, and dementia from the labels of three estrogen patches. (The Guardian)

Pope Leo XIV is kicking off a three-nation tour of Latin America, 3 weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question. (AP)

After three rejections, the FDA will again review a new drug application for the investigational combination of rivoceranib plus camrelizumab for the first-line treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma, Elevar Therapeutics announced.

Karyopharm Therapeutics, which brought the selective inhibitor of nuclear export drug selinexor (Xpovio) to market for multiple myeloma, filed for bankruptcy and announced plans to merge with Ayrmid Ltd.

The Association for Clinical Oncology (ASCO) said oncologists treating Medicare patients will face a roughly 2% pay cut under the 2027 Physician Fee Schedule from CMS.

ASCO also said it's monitoring the potential impact on cancer care delivery after flooding by heavy monsoon rains led to the closure of a facility in India that manufactures sterile injectable generic oncology medications.

Can breath tests detect cancer? (Washington Post)

Prosecutors dropped charges against Kseniia Petrova, the Russian researcher who was detained for months when she came to the U.S. with frog embryos to be used in cancer research. (The Guardian)

Subtype-specific mutations may drive relapse risk in B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, according to a report from the Children's Oncology Group. (Blood)

Women who have undergone a double mastectomy to treat ductal carcinoma in situ may not benefit from routine mammograms or other breast imaging. (UCLA Health)

More than 20,000 patients in the U.K. will trial cutting-edge blood tests to detect early-stage cancers. (The Independent)

Cancer survivors with obesity and a high genetic disposition to carry excess weight had a higher risk of second obesity-related cancers, according to a prospective cohort study. (JAMA Network Open)

A new, less-invasive swab test could make it easier and less painful to diagnose endometrial cancer. (Washington Post)

Newly approved pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib (Rasonque) has already generated $198 million in sales, according to maker Revolution Medicines.

The first patient to receive an mRNA vaccine designed to treat the stage II pancreatic cancer that might have killed her is thriving 7 years later. (NPR)

Surgery was linked with better survival compared with stereotactic ablative radiotherapy for early-stage non-small cell lung cancers where either approach was feasible, a target emulation trial found. (Journal of Clinical Oncology)

In patients who underwent endoscopic mucosal resections for large colorectal polyps, rectal lesions were linked to a higher likelihood of invasive cancer and recurrence compared with colonic lesions, a retrospective cohort study from Poland found. (Gut)

The American Society of Hematology developed new reference ranges for children and adults with Duffy-null status, a common genetic trait associated with naturally lower circulating white blood cell counts. (Blood Advances)
