#5699. Most people haven’t heard of kratom. What is it, and who’s using it?

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Over the last few years, the kratom plant and supplements made from it have garnered increasing attention from public health leaders. This broad category of products, which largely skirts any regulation, has seen major surges in potency, while becoming omnipresent on smoke shop and gas station shelves. Health officials have warned that concentrated compounds like 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) are an emerging public health threat, and federal policies to limit their availability are pending. In the meantime, multiple states and smaller localities have issued emergency bans on 7-OH, and in some cases, on all kratom products.

Despite the messaging and rising use, few Americans are familiar with kratom or the newer derivative products. They’re made with compounds that have scientific names like 7-OH, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI) and dihydro-7-hydroxy mitragynine (MGM-15) but are often sold on shelves with names like Dozo Perks, Roxy, and UltraOhmz Pseudo Supreme. New survey data from the Annenberg Public Policy Center show about two-thirds (66%) of Americans have never heard of kratom. Among those who had at least some familiarity, few understood the difference between its natural leaf form and more synthetic products.

That confusion carries over to the associated risks. In the survey of nearly 2,000 people, 66% were unsure if kratom products posed a serious public safety hazard. And most people didn’t understand health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s stance on regulation — a question that’s become complicated by repeated reports of kratom industry lobbying influence on the DEA’s proposed action.

STAT spoke with researchers and people who use or have used kratom and 7-OH to get a full picture of what these products are, along with their potential risks and benefits.

To an untrained eye, a kratom leaf might resemble a bay leaf. It grows on evergreen trees indigenous to Southeast Asian countries, including Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia. For centuries, people there have chewed the leaf or brewed it into tea for its stimulant-like effects.

Kratom (pronounce it with a hard or soft “a,” your choice) contains dozens of alkaloids, but mitragynine is the most abundant and the best understood. It acts as a partial agonist that binds to mu-opioid receptors in the nervous system. (Partial agonists produce less of a response from the receptor than full agonists, such as fentanyl or oxycodone.)

The first kratom products to arrive in the U.S. were made by drying and grinding up those leaves to create a matcha-like powder often used as a tea or swallowed in a capsule. In low quantities, it acts as a mild stimulant that can appear similar to coffee. In higher doses, people have used kratom to stave off chronic pain and even to help ease withdrawal from opioids. (There are no evidence-based dose recommendations, and there’s a lot of variation in both product potency and personal preference.)

“We call it swamp water, so that should give you a good visual,” said Madalyn Sklar, who uses kratom to ease chronic pain caused by degenerative disc disease, and hosts two podcasts on kratom. The first time Sklar drank the bitter tea made from kratom powder, she added orange juice as a sweetener, but still “it was so gross that I almost puked.” She’s taken it nearly every day since 2019, and says the results are better than when she was on meds like OxyContin and gabapentin.

She takes two teaspoons of powder — which works out to about 70-75 milligrams of mitragynine — every six hours. For her, there’s no high or euphoria. But she can do simple tasks that she couldn’t before, such as walk her dog and bend down to pick up its poop.

Sklar hasn’t experienced withdrawal symptoms when she’s occasionally stopped taking kratom and returned to more traditional pain medication. Research is limited, but has found that up to around 38% of kratom users may develop use disorders. In studies, withdrawal from kratom has appeared mild on a scale that measures clinical opioid withdrawal, with symptoms like anxiety, fatigue, gastrointestinal issues, and restlessness.

Before semi-synthetic products came onto the scene, most public health concern around kratom was directed at extracts and tinctures, recalled Sklar. Many of these products still tout mitragynine as the active ingredient, but in much more concentrated volumes than the whole leaf powder — think 100 to 300 milligrams of mitragynine in a bottle of liquid the size of a 5-hour Energy. (There are currently no federal proposals that aim to regulate concentrated mitragynine products.)

“But people got really interested in the other alkaloids over time,” said Katherine Hill, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health who has studied kratom. “And specifically they got interested in 7-hydroxymitrogynine.”

The alkaloid 7-OH does not appear in the fresh kratom leaf that people in Southeast Asia chew, according to Hill. It shows up in the dried leaf powder products, in small amounts. It’s also a metabolite, meaning that when the body absorbs mitragynine, some of it turns it into 7-OH. Once inside the body, 7-OH, like mitragynine, is a partial agonist to the mu-opioid receptor.

The products made with 7-OH — including tablets, gummies, shots, and drink powders — are semi-synthetic; they contain artificially concentrated amounts of the compound. When the products first started popping up, they were often sold in tablets containing 12-14 milligrams, users said. Those can offer sedative effects and pain relief. But now, tablets containing 25, 50, and even 100 milligrams of 7-OH are available.

“The first time I heard of 7-OH, it was very negative,” said Twinkle VanFleet, who co-hosts a kratom podcast with Sklar.

While natural kratom products carry a risk of dependence and what’s thought to be mild withdrawal at low doses, there’s growing concern that concentrated 7-OH products are even more addictive, and that withdrawal can be as bad as coming off a traditional opioid. Hill is working on a study of 7-OH users that will look at both tolerance and withdrawal. But for now, the risks are mainly documented in case reports, series, and other anecdotal accounts.

VanFleet suffers from intense pain from an injury that led to complex regional pain syndrome, and she has a deep mistrust of the medical system. Kratom didn’t ease her symptoms, so she eventually tried 7-OH, and found comfort in what she calls “nibbles” of smaller tablets. She currently takes around 12 milligrams per day and worries about a ban by the Drug Enforcement Administration. Still, she shares concerns about the availability of higher-dose products.

“I do see both sides of a lot of this,” VanFleet said. “In my perfect world, there would be 3, 5, and 10 milligram tablets, period. If even that.”

Greg Kiesow had been sober from alcohol for nearly 20 years and retired for three days when he went into a smoke shop that was promoting 7-OH products. The shopkeeper had heard it was some sort of natural energy supplement, like coffee, and gave Kiesow a free sample of tablets. “I took it home, and I took it. And 10 to 15 minutes later, it wasn’t coffee. It was a very powerful opioid,” Kiesow said.

Kiesow said he quickly developed an addiction. After 10 months, which he described as an extremely isolated period spent sitting on his back porch watching the birds at his bird feeder, he began to taper himself off the products. A few weeks later, he formed Kratom Anonymous, which has 15 virtual meetings per week for people looking to quit.

As 7-OH gained popularity, newer synthetic products have continued to crop up, including some with concentrated levels of mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI), another metabolite of mitragynine. Over the summer, the DEA proposed a ban of MGPI at any quantity. But an updated proposal in October, pushed by a lobbyist for the American Kratom Association, would allow small amounts of the compound to show up in products. Instead of an outright ban, the DEA now proposes limiting both MGPI and 7-OH based on the ratio of those compounds to mitragynine in any given product.

The reason for the change, according to the DEA, is that trace amounts of MGPI could appear in natural kratom. But the safety of small amounts is unclear. Test results presented in recent wrongful death lawsuits suggest that a natural kratom powder product, used by somebody who died after taking it, was likely contaminated with MGPI.

As more people use kratom and other associated products, there’s a growing recognition of the potential risk for addiction. Over 10 years, the National Poison Data Center found a 1,200% increase in kratom-related exposure reports — from 258 in 2015 to 3,434 in 2025. That includes all types of products. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say, over the last year, they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular.

But data on the most serious risks — overdose and death — are murky. The poison center data showed 233 deaths over the decade, most of which involved other substances like opioids, benzodiazepines, stimulants, and alcohol. (Researchers believe kratom can exacerbate the danger of a drug like fentanyl, and even more common medications like certain antidepressants.) A 2023 investigation by the Tampa Bay Times found that, over nearly 10 years, more than 580 people in Florida alone died from overdoses that involved kratom products.

Because both 7-OH and MGPI are metabolites of mitragynine, it can be difficult to draw conclusions about a given death, even with toxicology data. Complicating the matter even further: When tested, many kratom products — natural and synthetic — are found to have different concentration levels than the labels advertise, and some have been found to contain compounds that were not on the label at all.

Sklar and VanFleet are both proponents of regulations, not bans, on all types of kratom-related products. Others who advocate for natural kratom are working hard to distance themselves from the more synthetic products.

“Any who unwittingly support every concentrated 7-OH product are not defending the natural kratom plant. It may be helping to destroy it,” Mac Haddow, the American Kratom Association’s lobbyist, said in a recent video. “The solution is not to defend everything. The solution is to draw a clear, bright line.”

But others said they’ve suffered from taking natural kratom products, too. Danelle Kawasaki first tried kratom at a dry bar in her Montana town. It came at room temperature, and was advertised as a natural, herbal tea. The concoction eased her anxiety, making her feel both calm and energetic, able to speak with anyone she wanted. At first it was a weekly treat, then a few times a week. After a few months, she was having two drinks per day. She’d wake up with a jolt of anxiety, which she attributes to the tea not being in her system overnight. Without more, she’d be sick, crawling to the bathroom to puke.

It frustrates Kawasaki when people try to tell her that 7-OH, not natural kratom, is the problem. “This argument comes up all the time and it drives me nuts,” she said. “I know what was going on — it was the actual kratom tea powder. It wasn’t a concentrated form.”

At one point, she was drinking nearly 140 ounces of the tea per day. When she finally stopped, cold turkey, the withdrawal was its own dayslong nightmare.

Now, she advocates that the Fort Peck tribe, of which she’s a member, ban kratom on the reservation. For Kawasaki, “the risks outweigh the remedy that people are searching for.”

#5698. EXCLUSIVE: Ryan Serhant Warns Homebuyers Against Waiting for 2027: ‘You Don’t Want to Wait Until It’s Too Late’

Ryan Serhant is warning would-be homebuyers against assuming that lower mortgage rates will deliver an easier path to homeownership in 2027—and says the housing market has a problem that cheaper borrowing alone cannot solve.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Serhant shared his outlook for the year ahead, identified markets he believes could surprise buyers, and weighed in on the debate over private listings.

He also offered a glimpse inside his own townhouse and revealed a buyer request that has him searching for an enormous stretch of land with its own airport.

At the center of his housing outlook is a concern about people at opposite ends of the property ladder being unable to move.

“We have entered an environment where people can't afford to buy their first home, and their parents can't afford to leave their last one, and it's a problem we need to solve," he said.

“Lower mortgage rates will help, but rates alone are not going to fix the cost of housing or the cost of moving. We need to create more supply and fewer obstacles," Serhant added.

Serhant argued that the system has become an obstacle to moving, with consequences that have developed over many years.

“I think that what we've created is a environment, that is punishing mobility. Instead of rewarding mobility. And this was set up a long, long time ago. We didn't get here overnight.”

“Like, the housing market and the system we operate in rewards stability, because what's… it makes everyone feel comfortable. But then when that stability does not move, because stability is stability, mobility is mobility. Then everyone gets angry, and that's the environment that we're currently in.”

For his outlook, he is watching whether households have both the confidence and the resources to act.

“I think I'm watching employment, and I'm watching household confidence right now. I think pent-up demand only becomes a transaction when people have the confidence and the financial ability to act, and we'll see if that happens anytime soon.”

For people who can afford to buy but are considering waiting for a better deal in 2027, Serhant pointed to opportunities he believes already exist.

“I think in a lot of markets, we've entered a buyer's market now. You have the ability to negotiate in markets that you haven't been able to negotiate in in the past couple years.”

“I think there's a great opportunity to use the rate pressure that we have to negotiate closing costs, to negotiate rate buy-downs, to negotiate lower purchase prices, to get a house that really, really, really works for you. Remember, it is such an old and annoying saying, but you do marry the house, and you do date through the rates.”

His argument rests on the potential trade-off between borrowing costs and competition, although his comments about future rates and inventory are predictions.

“The market does become very stagnant. Interest rates should come down, and remember, you can refinance. And you should use the opportunity right now, if you can afford it, to purchase in a high-interest rate environment, because there's less competition.”

“Everyone wants low rates, they never want what comes with it. You know what'll happen if rates come down? There will be no houses for sale.”

“You won't even have the opportunity to complain about a high monthly payment. You won't even be able to talk about—the lack of affordability. You won't be able to complain, because there will be nothing for sale, because the demand is so great. There is not nearly enough houses for the demand we have in this country. Every 40-year-old who still lives at home will then move.”

Serhant also argued that the circumstances accompanying lower rates can make buyers reluctant to purchase.

“And what also brings down low interest rates is job insecurity. You know, is unemployment, is war. Are things that happen in the global environment that will make people, not confident to go and make a massive purchase. And so, you might miss that opportunity, too.”

He used the early months of the pandemic to illustrate his point about confidence and timing.

“In the spring of 2020, that was a great time to buy. But no, we had COVID, 'You can't buy. There's a death ticker on the bottom of every TV screen. You might not live.' You didn't take advantage of this environment, and then when the market came back, it was too late.”

“And so, I would use this moment to move quickly, because when things do even out, and they always do, markets go up and markets go down. Always. And forever. You don't want to wait until it's too late.”

Serhant highlighted returning city residents and investment in jobs as themes behind his market picks.

“I think people are returning to cities in a way that we haven't seen before. It's one of the reasons we just were launching, officially Chicago. This coming Wednesday. I'm incredibly excited about that.”

“The demand and the volume we've seen from all of our other Serhant markets wanting to move back to Chicago, who moved out over the past couple years. Taking advantage of good value, like we just talked about, is really exciting.”

“And I think places where you're seeing incredible job growth. Areas like Ohio, where there's major, major tech investment, not just in data centers. In office. And in manufacturing.”

“We have a lot of investment that's going into Western Pennsylvania, and, you're also seeing a lot of movement into Alabama.”

“You know, I think there are markets that will really, really surprise you because of great quality of life for the best cost structure the country has to offer.”

Away from the business of buying and selling, Serhant shared the first thing he does when he walks into his townhouse.

“I yell out my daughter's name. I wanted to see where she is in my house. We have a townhouse, so I'm trying to figure out which floor she's on, so I can, you know, prepare.”

His favorite spaces include a gym on the lower level, although his affection extends to the whole property.

“I have a pretty awesome gym. In the lower level that I built out, that's really, really cool, and I think that's pretty awesome, but I mean, I built it with my bare hand. It was a TV show that we did for Bravo about our renovation, and I love that house. Whole thing is great.”

He also described the practical details that help make his kitchen work, starting with a concealed ladder for reaching high cabinets.

“We have incredibly high ceilings. So we have a hidden ladder in our kitchen that looks like the baseboard under the kitchen. Island, and it pops out with the touch of your toe.”

“And, the ladder shows up, and so for anyone, you know, you know, who's vertically challenged to be able to reach upper cabinetry without having a ladder in front of your face at all times, so that you can still enjoy all that light and sunshine and high ceilings, I think is key.”

“Probably the greatest things that we have also in that kitchen are touchless, so, like, the sink, you know, you're cooking, and your hands are messy, and you're always hitting the thing. We have the kitchen sink, where all you have to do is tap it, and it turns on.”

“And so you just hit it with the back of your hand, and it turns on. So you're not, like, also getting the sink and the faucet dirty.”

“And then the same thing for the kitchen refrigerator and freezer. All you do is you slowly kind of, like, tap it with your elbow, or with the side, so you're not, like, yanking on anything, and it automatically just reveals itself to you. I think those little touches are overlooked.”

Among the unusual requests Serhant receives, one current search involves a vast amount of land—and a private airport.

“They're all wild. I'm dealing with somebody right now that wants 100,000 acres of land, which is impossible, for the most part."

For all the features a buyer might want, Serhant has one clear priority when choosing a home.

“You can change everything about the house you want over the years, you can grow into it, you can grow out of it, you can update it, you can paint it, you can flip it upside down. Unless you are Ken Griffin, and you can pick up a house, and you can move it, for the most part. Change the location.”

“And so, you always buy location first. Whatever that is, wherever that place is you want to be for the next 5-10 years, and most times you're paying more. But no one ever paid too much. And regretted it years later. Very, very rarely does that happen.”

“Remember, if you buy a trophy, you get to sell a trophy. If you buy a discount, because you're cheap, you will have to sell a discount. And you will feel cheap.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5697. Measles update: Wisconsin reports first measles-associated death since 1990

Measles update: Wisconsin reports first measles-associated death since 1990" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

The deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family."

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to New York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they said.

"Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

#5696. Opinion: AI depends on medical records that don’t always tell the full truth about women

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Annemarie G. Hirsch and Jennifer Silva

Hirsch and Silva are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

In September, the Gallup-Pivotal Women’s Health Survey reported that 34% of U.S. women strongly or somewhat agreed that a health care provider minimized or dismissed their symptoms in the past five years. Thirty-three percent reported being misdiagnosed or unable to get a diagnosis, compared with 21% of men reporting these experiences.

Medical records tell a different story. An epidemiologist and a sociologist, we recently released a study where we paired electronic medical records with detailed interviews with 87 women. We talked to these women about their pain and illnesses, work, family, poverty, violence, and encounters with the health care system.

Fifty-three of the women described a trust-breaking encounter with a health system, but only seven of them had medical records that documented mistrust. Thirty-two women reported experiencing a misdiagnosis, but misdiagnosis was only documented for eight of these women. Thirty women reported that they felt that clinicians treated them with disrespect, but this was not documented in the records anywhere.

For more than a decade, Kate lived with debilitating pelvic pain. Her doctors repeatedly attributed her symptoms to obesity. Her medical record reflected these assumptions.

When Kate underwent bariatric surgery and lost a significant amount of weight, her clinical notes became optimistic.

However, her symptoms persisted. Medical records pivoted from linking symptoms from obesity to mental health factors.

“Gastrointestinal malfunctions arising from mental factors.”

The turning point came only after Kate attended an appointment with her new husband. In the clinical notes, the provider documented Kate’s husband’s concerns:

For the first time in 10 years, doctors conducted the exams needed to finally diagnose Kate with endometriosis.

Kate’s medical record accurately documented years of conversations about weight and mental health. What it failed to capture was equally important: the cost of years spent with an undiagnosed disease, the frustration of not being believed, and the erosion of trust that occurs when symptoms are repeatedly explained away rather than investigated. Kate told us, “If I was tired, it was because I was overweight. If I had cramps, it was because I was overweight. Migraines, I was overweight. … They’re not hearing what you’re saying, and that compounded the issues that were going on.”

We often think of medical records as objective accounts of a patient’s health. They are not. Medical records are narratives, shaped by the questions clinicians ask and the assumptions they bring into the room. Medical record data reflect clinical decisions as well as biology. The language clinicians use and the details they choose to record can reinforce stereotypes that follow patients from one encounter to the next, influencing how future clinicians interpret symptoms, assess credibility, and make treatment decisions.

Medical record data also reflect what patients feel comfortable disclosing. What women share with their doctors depends on how much they trust them and how safe they feel. When people fear judgment, dismissal, or not being believed, important parts of their stories may remain unspoken, and thus, undocumented.

This fear may why 53 women in our data described a trust-breaking clinical encounter in their interview, while only seven of their medical records noted their mistrust. This is particularly a problem for women, who feel the pressure to be pleasant and pliant with doctors for fear of not being taken seriously.

Across the country, clinics and hospitals are adopting AI scribes that transcribe recorded interactions between doctor and patient and produce a clinical note. AI tools can be used to search and synthesize medical records to help with diagnostics and treatment plans, some with great success.

However, these tools are only as good as the data in the medical record. If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.

For AI to achieve its full potential in women’s health, medical records need to tell the complete story. Health care settings must be safe spaces where women can tell their stories; clinicians need to listen to women, even when their experiences do not fit clinical expectations; and clinicians need to document in the medical record when diagnoses are delayed or incorrect, without fear of being penalized.

Armed with these data, AI has the potential to do more than replicate biases of the past. AI could help identify patterns of missed diagnoses, reduce disparities in care, and ensure that more women are heard.

Annemarie G. Hirsch, Ph.D., M.P.H., and Jennifer Silva, Ph.D., are authors of “Seen But Not Heard: What Medical Records Don’t Tell Us About Women’s Lives.”

#5695. Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver

Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.

Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.

How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver

To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.

The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.

To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.

The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.

When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.

The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.

These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.

Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.

"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.

In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.

The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.

Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease

Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.

"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.

The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on new broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act."

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters."

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP says that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment."

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker said that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker said in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them."

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#5692. NASA’s Artemis I mission reveals surprising radiation levels near the Moon

NASA's Artemis I mission has provided new insights into how much cosmic radiation astronauts may encounter near the Moon compared with low Earth orbit. Using experimental detectors made from lithium fluoride crystals aboard the Orion spacecraft, researchers have obtained preliminary measurements that reveal unexpected differences in radiation exposure between the two environments.

During the uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022, Orion traveled around the Moon carrying more than 10,000 tiny crystals embedded inside two human-shaped mannequins. These devices recorded radiation exposure throughout the journey. Among them were several dozen experimental fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors created by scientists at the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) in Cracow. The researchers have now described a new method for analyzing the information stored in these crystals, offering insights into both cosmic radiation levels and the performance of the detectors. Their findings were published in the journal Radiation Measurements.

"The fluorescent radiation dose detectors based on lithium fluoride, developed at our institute, are passive in nature. In other words, they work like photographic film: once the crystals have been exposed to radiation, the tracks left by individual particles must be analyzed optically under a microscope," explains Prof. Pawel Bilski (IFJ PAN), one of the co-authors of the paper.

How Tiny Crystals Detect Cosmic Radiation

The lithium fluoride detectors work by capturing microscopic changes caused by radiation. When electrically charged particles pass through a crystal, they disrupt its internal atomic structure, creating defects known as color centers. Scientists can later illuminate the crystal with blue light, causing these altered regions to glow red. By examining that fluorescence under a microscope, researchers can identify the paths taken by individual radiation particles.

The detectors were part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study conducted during Artemis I. Several dozen experimental lithium fluoride detectors were placed inside both mannequins, including some containing high concentrations of the lithium-7 isotope. The contribution from IFJ PAN extended beyond these experimental devices. Its scientists also supplied nearly 600 thermoluminescent crystal detectors, which use a different technique to measure radiation exposure.

One major advantage of the new lithium fluoride detectors is that they simplify the process of examining radiation tracks. Traditional passive detectors made from plastic require chemical etching before scientists can study the marks left by incoming particles. Lithium fluoride crystals eliminate that step, allowing researchers to inspect the tracks directly with a standard fluorescence microscope.

As a result, observing the radiation tracks collected near the Moon was relatively straightforward. The more difficult task was determining exactly what those tracks revealed about radiation exposure. To obtain reliable numerical measurements, the team had to develop sophisticated calibration and analysis techniques.

Why Measuring Deep Space Radiation Is So Difficult

Unlike the controlled conditions of a laboratory, cosmic radiation is highly unpredictable. In a typical physics experiment, researchers can expose a detector to a beam containing a known type of particle with a specific energy and direction. In space, radiation arrives from every direction and includes many different particles and atomic nuclei traveling across an enormous range of energies.

This complexity makes the microscopic tracks difficult to interpret. Because incoming particles strike the crystals at different angles, their tracks extend in multiple directions. A microscope captures the section of each track within its focal plane (approximately one micrometer in size), but it also records a blurry glow from portions outside that narrow region. This additional light influences the measured fluorescence intensity, which scientists use to estimate how densely a particle ionizes the material.

Different particles also produce very different track patterns. Those that cause strong ionization leave continuous, sharply defined lines, while particles that produce weaker ionization may appear as scattered, disconnected dots. These differences further complicate the task of translating fluorescence measurements into meaningful radiation data.

To overcome these challenges, the researchers introduced several corrections and developed software capable of removing unwanted background signals. The improved analysis brought their measurements into close agreement with results from established detector technologies while also revealing radiation events that older devices could not detect.

"After applying a series of corrections and developing software to appropriately remove the background interfering with the measurements, our results differed by no more than 15% from those obtained using conventional track detectors across the entire overlapping range of energy deposition values. Moreover, we also recorded numerous particle tracks corresponding to energy deposits below the detection threshold of the detectors used to date," Prof. Bilski emphasizes.

Artemis I Reveals a Surprising Difference in Moon Radiation

The Artemis I measurements also allowed researchers to compare radiation exposure near the Moon with findings from an earlier experiment aboard the International Space Station.

More than a decade before Artemis I, the MATROSHKA experiment investigated radiation exposure using human-shaped mannequins on the space station. Some of the radiation recorded during that mission came from low-energy protons trapped within Earth's Van Allen radiation belts. As these particles traveled into the mannequins, they deposited energy at different depths, producing an uneven distribution of radiation doses.

Conditions near the Moon are substantially different. The Van Allen belts do not extend into the lunar environment, so the radiation encountered there contains a greater contribution from high-energy particles originating elsewhere in the galaxy.

These galactic particles carry enough energy to travel through the entire human body, releasing only a portion of their energy as they pass. Consequently, the Artemis I detectors recorded radiation doses that were distributed almost uniformly throughout the mannequins, unlike the uneven patterns observed in the earlier space station experiment.

The researchers also identified a finding that may seem counterintuitive. Although astronauts near the Moon are exposed to more radiation than those in low Earth orbit, the difference is not necessarily as dramatic as might be assumed.

"Low-energy protons, trapped by our planet's magnetic field within the Van Allen belts, can account for the majority of the radiation dose received by astronauts in low Earth orbit. In the vicinity of the Moon, this substantial contribution disappears. Our measurements from the MARE experiment indicate that, although total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than those in Earth orbit due to the considerable levels of galactic radiation, the difference is not as large as one might intuitively expect," Prof. Bilski notes.

New Radiation Detectors Could Help Protect Future Astronauts

The fluorescent lithium fluoride detectors aboard Artemis I were manufactured using the Czochralski method, a technique for growing crystals. Scientists at IFJ PAN first developed the technology about a decade ago and have continued refining it ever since.

Their compact size is one of their most useful features. Measuring just a few millimeters rather than several centimeters (on the order of millimeters rather than centimeters), the detectors are small enough to be worn comfortably by people, making them practical for monitoring radiation exposure during space missions.

They also provide sharper images of particle tracks than conventional plastic detectors that require chemical etching. This improved resolution allows scientists to distinguish individual tracks even when radiation doses are relatively high. In addition, the crystals can register a broad variety of particle types and energies, potentially providing a more complete picture of the radiation environment.

Another advantage is their ability to detect neutrons, particularly when the crystals are enriched with the lithium-6 isotope. When neutrons interact with lithium nuclei, they can trigger nuclear reactions that generate secondary charged particles. These particles leave detectable changes in the crystal, much like other forms of ionizing radiation.

Together, these capabilities make lithium fluoride detectors a promising tool for studying the complex radiation environment beyond Earth. The measurements from Artemis I offer a clearer picture of how cosmic radiation behaves near the Moon and demonstrate how compact detectors could help scientists evaluate radiation exposure during future missions.

The research conducted as part of the MARE project was supported by a grant from the National Science Centre, Poland (NCN), under its OPUS program.

#5690. An 18th-Century Connecticut Estate With ‘Little Women’ Ties Lists for $1.5 Million—Hidden Treasures Included

An 18th-century antique home in Wolcott, CT, with ties to a famous clockmaker and the Trans-Siberian Orchestra just hit the market for $1.5 million.

Listed for the first time in decades, the 1.94-acre property known as Spindle Hill includes a 5,360-square-foot primary residence, a hand-hewn barn, a manor home, an a history of treasure-filled walls.

"When you walk into the original section of the home, you feel the history," says listing agent Donna Membrino of William Pitt Sotheby’s International Realty. "The keeping room has an original beehive oven and a wooden mantel."

The property’s origins date to the early 1700s, when the land was purchased by the town’s first settler, the patriarch of the Alcott family, according to Membrino. Nathaniel Lane and Millicent Alcott Lane, the uncle and aunt of "Little Women" author Louisa May Alcott, later developed it into a working farm that stayed in the Lane family for generations.

The property is also linked to famed clockmaker Seth Thomas, who launched his first clockmaking venture from his childhood home just down the road.

“It was very important to the seller to preserve the home’s history, and they have taken great pains to do that,” Membrino says.

Marlene Tosun, who grew up on Spindle Hill Farm, became the owner of the property in the 1950s.

After moving in, she uncovered a series of hidden treasures: a violin beneath the floorboards of the main house; Nathaniel Lane’s diary, containing his handwritten business accounts, tucked behind a wall; and tomahawk heads embedded in the estate’s original hand-stacked stone walls, which are believed to have been built by Native Americans.

Membrino said the family also discovered a pair of 1700s wheels from Lane’s ox-drawn wagon, which was used to deliver goods to early New England customers.

The seller, Marlene’s daughter Sylvia Tosun, was once the lead vocalist for the Trans-Siberian Orchestra. She also featured on an international EDM hit championed by DJ Armin van Buuren.

In a meticulous restoration, Tosun set out to preserve the property’s original charm and character while bringing it up to modern luxury standards.

Original weathered wood salvaged from older, dismantled sections of the house was used to detail the Grand Salon. Other highlights include a black-and-white marble foyer, a 50-foot turret with an antique Schonbek chandelier, double-height cathedral ceilings, reclaimed wide-plank heart pine floors, a handcarved Italian marble chimneypiece, and three wood-burning fireplaces.

A modernized kitchen with Shaker cabinetry and granite countertops flows into a sunny dining room. Upstairs, the primary suite has a private terrace. The walk-out garden level features a wet bar and a “grand fireplace lounge” that serves as a professional recording studio.

The property also offers twin gazebos, a sunken patio, fruit trees and vegetable gardens, as well as “rare legal multi-family zoning” that allows for three private dwellings.

“Wolcott is a great town,” Membrino adds. “It’s close to Waterbury and Hartford but has more of a country feel, and it’s centrally located between New York and Boston.”

Buyers should note that “the antique barn is being sold in as-is condition,” according to the listing.

#5688. Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age

Muscles naturally become weaker as we get older, but scientists have discovered that some of the changes associated with aging may actually help protect muscle cells from damage. New research reveals why aging muscles shift toward a different type of muscle fiber and identifies a crucial molecule that could offer a new approach to treating muscle loss.

Muscle tissue contains bundles of fibers with different functions. Fast-twitch fibers produce powerful, rapid movements but fatigue relatively quickly. Slow-twitch fibers, by contrast, support sustained activity and contain higher concentrations of mitochondria, the cellular structures responsible for producing much of the energy muscles need.

As people age, muscle strength declines and mitochondria become less efficient. Surprisingly, aging muscles also develop a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibers, even though these fibers depend heavily on the very mitochondria that are losing their ability to function. Researchers have observed similar changes in several conditions that cause muscle wasting.

This raises an important question: Why would muscles increasingly rely on an energy-producing system that is becoming less effective?

A Crucial Molecule Linked to Muscle Aging

To investigate this puzzle, scientists focused on cardiolipin, a specialized fat molecule located almost exclusively within the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin helps maintain the membrane's distinctive folded architecture, which is essential for proper mitochondrial activity.

When cardiolipin is lacking, mitochondria struggle to generate sufficient energy. They also become less capable of producing the chemical signals and essential materials that cells require to function.

The researchers discovered that cardiolipin levels decrease in muscle mitochondria from both mice and humans as they age or experience disease. This decline was accompanied by structural abnormalities in the mitochondria and a loss of normal function.

To determine whether reduced cardiolipin directly contributes to these changes, rather than simply occurring alongside them, the team experimentally lowered cardiolipin levels in young mice.

The results closely resembled what happens during natural aging. Muscle fibers shifted away from the fast-twitch type toward slow-twitch fibers, matching the pattern previously observed in older mice and humans.

Even more strikingly, restoring cardiolipin to approximately two-thirds of its normal concentration began reversing muscle wasting and completely prevented the premature deaths seen in the affected animals.

Why Aging Muscles Sacrifice Strength for Protection

Further experiments revealed an unexpected explanation for the transformation. Rather than representing only a breakdown in muscle function, the shift toward slow-twitch fibers appears to be a protective response.

When cardiolipin concentrations fall, damaged mitochondria produce much larger quantities of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These highly reactive molecules can harm cellular structures, but they also play an important role in signaling that something is wrong.

The researchers found that ROS help initiate the transition from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers. When they treated muscle cells lacking cardiolipin with an antioxidant to reduce ROS, the transformation became less pronounced.

A protein known as ERRγ plays a central role in coordinating this response. It directs cells to reorganize their mitochondria and change their muscle fiber characteristics. When scientists inhibited ERRγ in muscle cells grown in the laboratory, the transition between fiber types stopped entirely.

The team also discovered how the newly remodeled fibers help defend themselves.

Mice with insufficient cardiolipin absorbed considerably more glucose from their bloodstreams. However, their muscles were not primarily using this additional sugar to produce energy.

Instead, experiments that tracked specially labeled glucose showed that muscle cells redirected the sugar toward manufacturing their own antioxidants. This helped protect them against the damaging effects of excess ROS.

"The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That's also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better," says Assistant Professor Fabian Finger, first and co-corresponding author, from the University of Copenhagen.

A Potential New Approach to Treating Muscle Wasting

Although the findings point toward possible treatments for age-related muscle decline, the experiments demonstrating the protective mechanism and reversal of muscle wasting were conducted in mice. Human muscle samples were used only to establish that cardiolipin levels also decrease with age in people.

Nevertheless, researchers already have some ways to influence cardiolipin.

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, a medication designed to help stabilize cardiolipin, for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. This suggests that targeting the molecule is medically feasible, although its effectiveness against ordinary age-related muscle loss remains unknown.

Another potential treatment target is ERRγ, the protein responsible for helping muscles adapt to mitochondrial stress.

ERRγ belongs to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors. These proteins are already established targets for approximately 10 to 15 percent of FDA-approved medications made from small molecules. Drugs that activate ERRγ are also being investigated in preclinical research for other medical applications.

The findings suggest that future therapies might work by restoring cardiolipin levels or by influencing the protective adaptations controlled by ERRγ.

"What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies," says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, Associate Professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen.

The research involved scientists from more than 20 institutions. It was led by the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen in collaboration with the Center for Adipocyte Signaling at the University of Southern Denmark.

Financial support came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, European Research Council, Lundbeck Foundation, US National Institutes of Health, and additional funding organizations.

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Congratulations on making it to the end of the week. This is Jonathan Wosen, STAT’s West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter. We’ve got an eclectic lineup for you today, including a look at how declining vitamin K shots are impacting infants, why medical records often don’t tell the full story about women’s health, and results on health and science-related ballot measures across the country.

Oh, and a study that unearths evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb (pun intended). Let’s dig in.

That’s how much higher the risk of brain bleeding during the first six months of life was in infants who didn’t receive a vitamin K shot, compared to those who did. Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K, which plays an essential role in forming blood clots. That’s why the American Academy of Pediatrics has for more than 60 years recommended that newborns get the one-time shot shortly after birth. But medical mistrust has led a growing number of parents to turn down the injection; the share of newborns who weren’t given vitamin K rose from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025.

That trend has had grim consequences, according to a study published Thursday in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Researchers looked back on data from more than 5 million infants born between 2017 and 2025 and found that, compared to infants given vitamin K, those who weren’t given K had a 47% higher risk of bleeding during their first six months and a 169% higher risk of dying while bleeding shortly after birth.

In recent years, the Kratom plant and related synthetic products have become omnipresent across smoke shops and gas station shelves, buoyed by proponents who extol these products’ pain-relieving powers. But public health experts have raised serious concerns about the potential dangers of kratom — and the fact that these products are not closely regulated.

It’s a debate that is confusing to many; two-thirds of Americans have never even heard of kratom. STAT’s Theresa Gaffney has you covered with this timely explainer on the drug. The piece covers how a plant that has been chewed and brewed for centuries in Southeast Asia due to its stimulant-like effects has quickly risen in popularity in the U.S., where some users say kratom has eased chronic pain and helped them get off opioids.

Theresa also digs into 7-OH and MGPI, semi-synthetic related products that some experts worry are especially addictive. Clinicians who run addiction treatment centers say that they’ve seen a rise in patients seeking help to get off 7-OH in particular. But for now, data on overdoses and deaths are murky.

You might think that your medical records are an objective account of your health. But they’re not, write epidemiologist Annemarie Hirsch and sociologist Jennifer Silva. The pair recently published a study in which they paired electronic medical records and interviews with 87 women about pain, illness, and encounters with the health care system.

Many of the women described trust-breaking encounters with health care providers and misdiagnoses, but these moments were rarely documented. The authors point to the story of a woman who lived with debilitating pelvic pain for more than a decade as a poignant example. Doctors at first dismissed her pain as related to obesity, pivoting to mental health after she lost weight. Notably, the turning point only came after her husband joined her for an appointment, and she was ultimately diagnosed with endometriosis. Her medical records chronicle this diagnostic odyssey, but they don’t capture the frustration and disillusionment she experienced after years of having her pain downplayed. Hirsch and Silva write that such stories raise concerns about the use of AI to advance women’s health.

“These tools are only as good as the data in the medical record,” they write. “If a woman’s symptoms are filtered through assumptions about her weight or mental health, and the true story of her pain is omitted, AI may learn and reproduce how the woman is framed in the record.”

Many Democrats are still celebrating the blue wave that handed their party control of both the House and Senate. But that momentum didn’t fully translate to health-related ballot initiatives across the country. As of late Thursday, voters in Arizona, Colorado, and Washington had approved or were on track to endorse measures that would prohibit transgender youth from participating on school sports teams aligned with their gender identity. Voters in four states with abortion-related ballot measures chose to preserve the status quo, with Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia choosing to maintain abortion rights while Idaho preserved the state’s existing ban.

Meanwhile, California voters appear on track to endorse Proposition 38, which would authorize $8.4 billion in bonds to fund immunology research. The measure has sparked controversy because its main backer is also the co-founder of an institute poised to receive half the funds. South Dakota voters rejected an amendment that would have conditioned a state Medicaid expansion on federal financial support holding steady. And Massachusetts voters can breathe easier (well, sort of) after a measure to repeal the state’s recreational marijuana law was defeated handily.

You can read more from me and Theresa Gaffney. But first, let’s stick with weed for a moment longer.

Early writing by the ancient Greek historian Herodotus — known for his foundational text on the Greco-Persian wars and banger quotes like, “of all possessions a friend is the most precious” — is a key source used by historians to support the idea that prehistoric communities were smoking weed. Archaeological evidence is hard to come by (plants are perishable!) and just as tricky to interpret. But a new paper, published yesterday in Science, offers compelling evidence of ritual cannabis use in a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb.

The monumental burial mound included a log cabin-like structure, one coffin, and the remains of multiple individuals and horse sacrifices. There, archaeologists found hundreds of cannabis seeds, a handful of which were analyzed and dated to the first decade of the eighth century BCE. But there was an even rarer finding: two long braids of human hair containing significant amounts of the psychoactive compound cannabinol. “Although proving intent in a prehistoric context will remain impossible,” the authors wrote, “the evidence is strongly in favor of intentional consumption for the plant’s psychoactive properties.”

Admittedly, this is not our usual fare. But the study is a good reminder that drug use is not a modern issue, but rather a phenomenon that’s been with us for millenia. — Theresa Gaffney

#5686. The Efficacy of Broad Match + Audiences Strategy in Real Estate

When considering digital marketing strategies, the realm of real estate is no different from any other industry. The key objective remains the same - reaching the target audience with an impactful, compelling message that can inspire action. An increasingly popular approach adopted by real estate agents is the broad match + audiences strategy. This approach leverages the power of Google AdWords' broad match feature and combines it with audience targeting to attain superior marketing results.

The real estate sector thrives on the availability of a vast array of properties, each with a unique combination of attributes that appeal to different prospective buyers. Recognizing this immense diversity and matching it with the correct buyer is a daunting challenge that real estate agents constantly grapple with. This is where the broad match + audiences strategy steps in, optimizing the process by expanding reach while ensuring relevance.

The broad match feature in Google AdWords is a type of keyword match that allows your ads to show whenever someone searches for that keyword or a related phrase. It can include searches that are misspellings, synonyms, related searches, and other relevant variations.

With the broad match feature, you're casting a wide net over an extensive range of search queries. It brings with it the advantage of gaining visibility across a wider spectrum of potential buyers who might not use the exact keywords that you've selected for your campaign.

In the real estate industry, property attributes can be incredibly diverse, ranging from "3-bedroom apartments in New York City" to "colonial-style houses with large gardens in Austin". By leveraging the broad match feature, agents can reach potential clients who use various search terms that directly or indirectly relate to their listing.

Audience targeting is a method used in digital marketing to segment audiences based on specific criteria like demographics, interests, buying behavior, etc. Google AdWords allows you to target your ads to specific audiences, ensuring they are seen by those who are most likely to be interested in your offerings.

In the context of real estate, audience targeting can be a game-changer. For instance, if an agent specializes in selling luxury homes, they can target audiences with high-income levels and a demonstrated interest in luxury living. Alternatively, if an agent focuses on properties suitable for first-time buyers, they can target younger audiences who have recently started searching for homes.

The marriage of broad match keywords with audience targeting may seem counter-intuitive at first, considering one aims at breadth and the other at specificity. However, the combination forms a robust strategy that takes the best of both worlds - wide reach and precise targeting.

The broad match feature ensures a wide reach, allowing real estate agents to surface their listings to a large number of prospective clients. But, broad match alone can lead to high impression counts with low conversion rates as the ads may be presented to irrelevant audiences. This is where audience targeting steps in to bring precision.

When used in conjunction, the broad match feature ensures that your ads reach a wide array of searchers, while audience targeting ensures these ads are shown to a specific subset of this wide audience who are most likely to be interested in your property listings.

This synergistic approach allows real estate agents to achieve two key objectives:

In the dynamic and competitive world of real estate, digital marketing strategies need to be both comprehensive and precise. The broad match + audiences strategy does precisely that - it maximizes the reach of property listings while maintaining relevance to the audience. As such, it is not surprising that this strategy is being widely adopted by savvy real estate agents seeking to gain a competitive edge in the digital realm. The power of a wide-reaching yet finely tuned marketing strategy should not be underestimated in a market as diverse and competitive as real estate.

#5685. CMS proposes rollbacks of 'excessively burdensome' Conditions of Participation

CMS proposes rollbacks of 'excessively burdensome' Conditions of Participation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services plans to trim several “unnecessary” requirements for hospitals and other providers participating in Medicare, including emergency services readiness requirements and staff training for obstetrical services that had been brought during the tail end of the Biden administration.

The proposed rule’s Conditions of Participation (CoP) rollbacks, shared late Thursday (PDF), followed a “comprehensive review” CMS conducted to identify and eliminate “obsolete, outdated and excessively burdensome regulations.”

Removing these, the agency estimated, would save $320 million and free up 3.26 million hours of staff time for provider organizations.

Among the chief changes is a repeal of requirements finalized in the 2025 Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) and ASC Payment Systems rule that tasked hospital and critical access hospital emergency departments to be “continually prepared” to provide emergency screening or stabilization regardless of whether they provide relevant specialty services, which were made effective in July 2025.

The 2025 rule paired those with baseline staffing and care delivery standards, annual staff training and maternal quality assessment and performance improvement (QAPI) requirements around obstetric care, which are currently set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027. CMS also proposed eliminating those requirements this week.

CMS under the prior administration had said these requirements would improve safety, quality and the timeliness of care delivery for pregnant women.

On the other hand, CMS' new proposed rule looks to add a new obstetrics requirement for hospitals and critical access hospitals tied to the collection of birth tissue, “including standards for informed consent and policies and procedures to support families requesting their birth tissues for cultural, religious or personal reasons,” per a fact sheet.

Other proposed changes to the CoPs include clarification revisions to policies regarding distance-related eligibility for critical access hospital designation and to implement an exemption from the distance eligibility requirements for some critical access hospitals.

Long-term care facilities would also see changes around COVID-19 vaccination education for staff and uptake for residents, as well as exemptions for existing facilities from newer room occupancy and bathroom facility standards. Among other changes are removals or slim downs of respiratory illness data reporting requirements for multiple types of provider facilities.

The proposed rule will be open for public comment for 60 days. Among these, CMS said it is interested in hearing from stakeholders on additional requirements for participating providers, including flexibilities for physician supervision of certified registered nurse anesthetists, expanding the scope of practice of nurse practitioners and physician assistants in long-term care facilities, and reducing barriers for new transplant programs to achieve initial certification.

#5683. Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal

Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.

Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.

"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."

A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems

The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.

The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.

"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."

New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated

The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.

The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.
