#5647. Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging

Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.

A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.

Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.

"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.

Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.

Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years

To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.

At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.

Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.

Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.

Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.

Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.

High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline

The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.

After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.

That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.

Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.

These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.

Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes

When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.

Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.

The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.

Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.

Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.

Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.

Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?

The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.

"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."

Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.

In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.

The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.

The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.

#5646. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

#5645. 5 Historic ‘Minimansions’ Under $400K Where You Get 3,000+ Square Feet for the Price of a Starter Home

If you’re in the market for a large home but have a limited budget, consider a house that needs some TLC.

For the ambitious investor who wants to roll up their sleeves and dive into a home improvement project, a historic home might just fit the bill.

From New York to Tennessee, we found five “minimansions,” each with more than 3,000 square feet of living space for the price of a starter home.

Magnolia Manor: Here’s a chance for an investor to transform this 1.28-acre legacy compound into a "hospitality destination" or investment property of their dreams, subject to applicable permitting.

Built in 1849 for Judge Austin Miller, the 4,228-square-foot estate, formerly a bed-and-breakfast, has a four-bedroom Greek Revival brick home with a covered front porch, a one-bedroom guest cottage, a potting house, a gazebo, and a detached two-car garage. Historic highlights include double parlors, original architecture, hardwood floors, chandeliers, oversized windows, and brick details.

Located in the North Main Street Historic District, the home needs some work, as reflected in the price, and is being offered as is.

Larry Childers of Childers Real Estate is the listing agent.

Italianate brick mansion: This "treasured" six-bedroom brick estate near the Mohawk River was built in 1860 and has had only two owners.

Two entrances, including one with original horse ties and carriage step, lead to the 4,192-square-foot home full of charm and character. Period details include a grand staircase, preserved hardwood floors, custom moldings, expansive windows, French doors, a butler's pantry, and an original marble fireplace. An original basement kitchen features a fireplace. A cupola provides panoramic waterfront views of the Mohawk Valley.

Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the home offers the next buyer the opportunity to enjoy a "living piece of American history."

Rebecca Zarski of Howard Hanna Delmar is the listing agent.

The A.M. Legg House: Built in 1913, this historic five-bedroom “architectural treasure” was once the home of former Pontiac Mayor Achalis Morris Legg.

The 3,715-square-foot estate has a covered front porch with original mosaic tile flooring, custom millwork, multiple French doors, preserved hardwood floors, elegant built-ins, four fireplaces, and a pocket door. Other amenities include a sunroom, a dining room with built-in cabinetry, a full walk-up attic with room for expansion, and a partly finished lower-level entertainment room with a bar and a canning room.

A detached two-car garage with a dual-access driveway is also on the property.

David R. Wayman of Eppel Realty is the listing agent.

Louis Bierbauer Brewery country estate: Sitting on 3.59 acres at the base of the Canajoharie Gorge, this picturesque four-bedroom compound is surrounded by original stone walls and sits along a creek.

Built in 1860, the thoughtfully updated 3,528-square-foot interior still has wood-paneled walls, stone details, and built-ins. Modern updates include radiant-heated floors, a kitchen with wood cabinetry and stainless-steel appliances, and a circular staircase. The primary suite has an exposed wood-beam ceiling and a decorative fireplace. An underground grotto “still exists where the beer vats were aged,” according to the listing, which also says the property is not in a flood zone.

A one-bedroom apartment could be used for multigenerational living or as an income-producing rental. A salon space with a dedicated entry could also be used for other business purposes.

Rochelle Monk of Krutz Properties is the listing agent.

Updated Victorian: Built in 1903, this five-bedroom home, originally owned by Delia and Henry Logan of Logan Automobile Co., has 3,180 square feet of carefully updated living space.

Time-honored details include original hardwood floors, period millwork, pocket doors, stained glass, formal living and dining rooms, and seven fireplaces. Updates include new windows, a remodeled kitchen with stainless-steel appliances and a breakfast bar, and a finished third-floor bonus level. A wraparound covered porch would be a nice spot to enjoy morning coffee.

A detached one-car garage is also on the fenced lot.

Blaine Ritchie of Coldwell Banker Select Properties is the listing agent.

#5644. Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

Eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an important role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake."

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow

The study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

The new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an important indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

The team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

"Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance."

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

During the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

The study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

Funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

#5642. Scientists discover a hidden driver of high cholesterol and a way to stop it

Heart disease linked to high cholesterol continues to be the leading cause of death worldwide. Although doctors have more treatment options than ever, many people still struggle to lower their cholesterol to safe levels. Others experience side effects that make existing medications difficult to take.

Researchers at the University of California San Diego School of Medicine have now identified a previously unknown biological pathway that helps explain why diets high in cholesterol can gradually weaken the body's ability to remove harmful low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol from the bloodstream. Even more promising, they have identified an experimental drug that has already undergone safety testing in humans and could potentially interfere with this process.

The findings, published in Nature, could open the door to a new approach to treating high cholesterol.

"We've known for a long time that a high-cholesterol diet reduces the liver's ability to clear cholesterol from the blood, but we didn't fully understand why," said senior author Alan Saltiel, PhD, professor of medicine at UC San Diego School of Medicine and director of the UC San Diego/UCLA Diabetes Research Center. "This new discovery explains a critical piece of that puzzle."

The liver plays a central role in controlling cholesterol levels. It removes cholesterol from the bloodstream so it can be processed, broken down, and used by other parts of the body.

To accomplish this, liver cells rely on structures called LDL receptors. Located on the surface of these cells, the receptors work much like docking stations, capturing LDL cholesterol circulating in the blood and bringing it inside for processing.

The number of available receptors matters. When liver cells have more LDL receptors, they can remove more cholesterol from circulation. This is one reason widely used cholesterol medications, including statins and PCSK9 inhibitors, are effective. They help maintain or increase the number of receptors available to clear LDL cholesterol.

Scientists Uncover a Hidden Cholesterol Pathway

Using experiments involving mice and human cells, the researchers discovered a previously unrecognized process that interferes with the liver's ability to clear cholesterol. Over time, this mechanism reduces the number of LDL receptors, making it harder for the body to keep blood cholesterol under control.

The process begins with a protein known as Ral, which Saltiel had previously investigated in fat cells. The team discovered that consuming high amounts of dietary cholesterol activates Ral, setting off a chain of events that leads to the loss of LDL receptors. As Ral activity increases, fewer receptors remain available to remove harmful cholesterol from the bloodstream.

The researchers then identified another critical piece of the mechanism: an enzyme called cathepsin A (CTSA). This enzyme helps drive the process responsible for depleting LDL receptors.

When scientists used a small molecule inhibitor to block CTSA, the results were striking. LDL receptors became more stable, and levels of circulating LDL cholesterol dropped dramatically in mice.

The discovery is especially significant because the newly identified pathway is different from those targeted by current cholesterol medications. That distinction could make it possible to develop treatments for patients who do not respond adequately to existing drugs.

"There's still a real need for new cholesterol-lowering options, since some people can't get to safe levels even with the drugs we have now," said Saltiel. "This new pathway we discovered is completely separate from anything that existing drugs target, so it gives us a new opportunity to fill that gap."

A Previously Tested Drug Could Accelerate Treatment

Discovering a new biological target is usually only the beginning of a lengthy drug development process. Researchers often need years of additional work to identify a suitable compound and determine whether it can be used safely in people.

In this case, however, the scientists may already have a promising candidate.

A drug designed to inhibit CTSA had previously been developed as a potential treatment for heart failure. Although the program was eventually discontinued for strategic reasons, the experimental medication had already progressed through a Phase 1 clinical trial, where it was successfully evaluated for safety in humans.

That earlier work could provide an important advantage. Rather than beginning drug development from scratch, researchers believe the existing CTSA inhibitor may be ready to advance into a Phase 2 clinical trial to investigate its effectiveness against high cholesterol.

The findings are still at an early stage, and the drug has not yet been shown to lower cholesterol in humans. Nevertheless, its previous clinical testing could shorten the path toward determining whether this new treatment strategy works in patients.

"Luckily, there's an experimental drug sitting on the shelf that's already been shown to be safe in humans," said Saltiel. "We hope to test whether this might be effective by conducting a clinical trial -- which could potentially bring a new treatment option to patients much sooner than would have been expected."

Co-authors of the study include Xue Feng, Shuo Zhang, Yuqi Wang, Twisha Kurlagunda, Allyssa Sit, Sadatsugu Sakane, Se Yong Park, Churaibhon Wisessaowapak, Kaylee Nguyen, Jamie Yan, Himani Pothulu, Catherine Dinh, Felicia Chu, Yuyao Ren, Bichen Zhang, Patrick Secrest, Chao-Wei Hung, Preethi Veeragandham, Yuliya Skorobogatko, Tatiana Kisseleva, and Amit R. Majithia at UC San Diego; Priya Jaishankar, Pusu Yang, and Adam Renslo at the University of California, San Francisco; Linmeng Han and Peng Zhao at the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio; and Philip L.S.M. Gordts at the University of Utah.

The research received partial funding from the National Institutes of Health (Grants P30DK063491, R01DK117551, R01DK128796, and R01DK135289) and an American Diabetes Association postdoctoral fellowship (1-25-PDF-76).

#5641. GLP-1s Are Changing America’s Kitchens—and Raising Questions About Its Trash

Open a custom bathroom vanity today, and you might find more than towels and toiletries: a refrigerator for medication, drawers for syringes, even a compartment for used-needle disposal.

Today, 1 in 5 U.S. households (21%) includes a current GLP-1 user—up from just 9% in January 2025, according to an analysis by PwC.

And now, America's homes appear to be developing a taste for less, too: The hidden kitchen is among the emerging trends in the National Kitchen & Bath Association's (NKBA) 2027 design forecast.

But the rise of injectable medications is also drawing attention to a less glamorous, often-overlooked part of domestic life: the trash.

In New York City, sanitation workers have reported a sharp increase in needlestick injuries. The Department of Sanitation has identified the growing use of injectable medications, including GLP-1s, as a possible contributor, although it doesn't track the types of needles involved.

On Nov. 9, the city will more than double fines for improperly discarded household medical waste, drawing objections from property owners who argue they have little control over what tenants throw away.

GLP-1 medications are said to reduce what's commonly called food noise: persistent, sometimes intrusive thoughts about food and eating. And as that mental chatter quiets, some households are finding they don't need quite as much food—or space to store and prepare it.

PwC's research on GLP-1 users found that grocery spending declined 5.5%, as users shifted away from snacks, sugary drinks, and alcohol in favor of produce, protein, and supplements. It's even prompting some homeowners to reconsider how much kitchen they want.

"While these grand kitchens aren’t going anywhere, we have seen an increase in customers selecting homes with more modest kitchen designs," Tammy Crosby, CEO of The House Designers, tells Realtor.com®.

The shift marks a stark departure from decades of kitchen design centered on abundance—perhaps nowhere more apparent than in the elaborate Tuscan-style kitchens of the early 2000s. Countertops doubled as displays for colorful bottles of infused oils, jars of preserved vegetables, and other culinary-themed decorations.

Even the modern farmhouse, which traded Old World ornamentation for a more restrained aesthetic, retained that appetite for excess: sprawling islands, oversized refrigerators, and walk-in pantries.

Now, Crosby says customers using GLP-1 medications are likelier to favor compact, efficient layouts that free up square footage for other priorities.

"A range will do just fine—no need for an expanded appliance suite with a separate cooktop and double wall ovens," she says.

Likewise, households purchasing less food may no longer need oversized refrigerators or separate pantries designed for bulk groceries.

But the move toward quieter kitchens isn't just about shrinking their footprints—it's really about reducing what homeowners see.

And the so-called invisible kitchen takes that philosophy a step further, concealing appliances, food storage, and preparation areas behind cabinetry to create a more seamless living space.

According to the NKBA 2027 Kitchen Trends Report, 81% of surveyed industry professionals believe dividing kitchens into functional zones is a practice that's here to stay, while 85% say cabinetry is being designed to conceal appliances and other working elements.

Of course, overlapping timelines doesn't establish that GLP-1s are driving those changes. But the parallel is striking: Just as the medications are said to mute the thoughts surrounding food, designers are finding ways to lessen its visual presence in the home.

A similar philosophy is finding its way into bathrooms: 72% of surveyed industry professionals expect bathrooms to expand to accommodate wellness activities and more efficient storage, according to NKBA 2026 Bath Trends Report.

That might mean a custom vanity with dedicated compartments for medications and personal-care supplies, or bathroom cabinetry that conceals a small medication refrigerator or sharps container.

But Crosby cautions against assuming that injectable medications will create widespread demand for bathroom refrigeration.

"There has been talk of some people requesting refrigeration in the bathroom to store GLP-1s, but that’s probably overhyped," she says, noting that people using insulin have long stored their medication in kitchen refrigerators.

Even as GLP-1s quiet food noise in American homes, discarded needles are causing a cacophony in the trash—as a sharp rise in needlestick injuries among New York City sanitation workers makes clear.

Such injuries have tripled in the Big Apple since 2023.

That year, the Department of Sanitation recorded 23 injuries, followed by 40 in 2024 and 50 in 2025. By Oct. 21 of this year, the number had climbed to 69, according to testimony at a City Council hearing.

Sanitation worker Nicholas Derenzi knows what one of those injuries can mean. While collecting garbage on a Bronx route in 2020, a discarded needle pierced his glove.

"I felt something prick through my glove," he told NY1 in August. "You're by yourself, and that's really when it kind of set in how scary, and the gravity of the situation."

Coworkers subsequently discovered multiple needles inside the trash bags, and Derenzi was taken to an emergency room.

While it may seem small—just a small pinprick afterall—these injuries pose a serious health risk, requiring medical evaluation and follow-up testing for bloodborne infections.

So, with needlestick injuries mounting, New York City is turning to higher fines to discourage improper disposal of household medical waste.

Beginning Nov. 9, the fine will rise from $100 to $250, the maximum permitted under the applicable city law. But the change has drawn pushback from property owners who argue they have little control over what residents discard.

"Owners generally have no control over what tenants or passersby place in trash bags or building receptacles," the Small Property Owners of New York (SPONY) wrote in a public comment opposing the rule.

The organization warned that expecting landlords or building staff to inspect garbage could expose them to the very injuries the regulation is intended to prevent.

DSNY, however, maintains that property owners already have a responsibility to ensure waste is disposed of properly.

"Property owners have always been responsible for the proper disposal of trash, and that includes using the proper containers and sorting material correctly," Vincent Gragnani, the department's press secretary, tells Realtor.com.

The new regulation specifies a $250 penalty for an individual violating the disposal requirements, although precisely how responsibility is determined when needles are discovered in a multifamily building's shared trash remains unclear.

Meanwhile, DSNY is also working to reduce direct contact with garbage through mechanized collection. Its new residential trash bins are compatible with equipment that lifts and empties them into collection trucks, reducing the need for sanitation workers to handle bags manually.

But those changes don't eliminate the need for safe disposal at the source.

"New York City residents disposing of syringes, needles, scalpels, lancets, and other sharp objects are legally required to place them in a 'sharps' container or other leak-proof, puncture-resistant container, such as a laundry detergent bottle," Gragnani says.

Once securely sealed and labeled "HOME SHARPS - NOT FOR RECYCLING," those containers can go into regular household trash. Residents can also bring used sharps to hospitals, nursing homes, or designated drop-off locations.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5640. Scientists finally discover how a common gut bacterium can trigger colon cancer

For nearly two decades, scientists have known that a common gut bacterium can produce a toxin that damages the colon and helps drive the formation of tumors. What they could not explain was how the toxin first attaches to intestinal cells and begins its attack. Now, researchers have uncovered that missing step, revealing a surprising vulnerability that could lead to new ways of protecting the colon.

The breakthrough comes from a team led by scientists at the Johns Hopkins Kimmel Cancer Center, its Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, and the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Their findings, published in Nature, identify a protein called claudin-4 as the essential docking point for a bacterial toxin known as BFT.

Even more promising, the researchers have already used this discovery to develop a molecular decoy that intercepts the toxin before it can damage colon cells. The strategy successfully protected mice from the toxin's harmful effects, suggesting a possible new approach to preventing bacterial damage associated with colorectal cancer. The research received partial support from the National Institutes of Health.

"We've made several attempts over time to identify the receptor, so this is an exciting moment," says senior author Cynthia Sears, M.D., Bloomberg~Kimmel Professor of Cancer Immunotherapy and professor of medicine at Johns Hopkins. "Understanding how bacterial toxins work can open doors to new approaches for detection and therapy for associated diseases, including diarrhea, colorectal cancer and bloodstream infections."

How a Common Gut Bacterium Can Promote Colon Cancer

The investigation centers on Bacteroides fragilis, a bacterium that can be found in the intestines of up to 20% of healthy people. Although the presence of this bacterium does not automatically mean someone will develop cancer, certain strains produce a powerful toxin capable of disrupting the colon's protective lining, causing inflammation, and encouraging tumor growth.

The toxin, known as B. fragilis toxin or BFT, has been under investigation for years. In a landmark 2009 study published in Nature Medicine, Sears and her colleagues demonstrated that the toxin could promote the development of colon tumors. Their work helped establish an important connection between toxin-producing gut bacteria, chronic inflammation, and colorectal cancer.

Earlier experiments also revealed that BFT damages a protein called E-cadherin, which helps hold neighboring cells together and maintain the colon's protective barrier. When this protein is broken apart, the barrier becomes compromised, potentially allowing harmful substances and bacteria to interfere with the surrounding tissue.

However, one critical question remained unanswered. Although BFT could break down E-cadherin, the toxin did not appear to attach directly to that protein. Researchers suspected that another molecule was helping the toxin reach its target, but repeated attempts to identify it had failed.

Scientists Identify the Missing Link Using CRISPR

To solve the mystery, the researchers turned to CRISPR, a powerful gene-editing technology that allows scientists to selectively disable genes and investigate what they do.

Maxwell White, an M.D./Ph.D. candidate working in Sears' laboratory, led a genome-wide CRISPR screening effort in collaboration with Matthew Waldor's laboratory at Harvard Medical School. The team systematically switched off genes in colon epithelial cells, the cells that form the inner lining of the colon, to determine which ones were necessary for the toxin to attach and cause damage.

One gene stood out dramatically. It produces claudin-4, a protein that helps neighboring cells form tight junctions, the seals that limit the movement of substances between cells and help maintain the intestinal barrier.

When the researchers disabled the gene responsible for claudin-4, BFT could no longer bind to the colon cells. Without that initial attachment, the toxin was unable to attack E-cadherin.

The finding revealed that claudin-4 acts as a receptor for the bacterial toxin. In effect, the toxin must first latch onto this protein before it can carry out its damaging activity.

"It took a while to get the assay working and validate the approach, but once we were able to do the screen, claudin-4 was a clear, resounding top hit," says White. "That was an exciting moment."

An Unexpected Discovery Reveals a New Bacterial Attack Strategy

The identity of the receptor surprised the scientists.

Sears and other researchers had expected BFT to interact with a protein involved in cellular signaling, such as a G protein-coupled receptor. These receptors act somewhat like communication switches, allowing cells to respond to signals from their surroundings.

Claudin-4, however, serves a very different purpose. Rather than functioning primarily as a signaling receptor, it helps maintain the physical connections between neighboring cells.

The discovery also revealed an unusual way for a bacterial toxin to operate. BFT belongs to a class of enzymes called proteases, which cut other proteins. Most proteases act directly on their targets, but BFT appears to require a separate receptor before it can reach and damage E-cadherin.

When the team reviewed previous scientific research, they could not identify another toxin known to use the same mechanism.

To establish that BFT and claudin-4 truly bind to each other, the Johns Hopkins researchers collaborated with structural biologists F. Xavier Gomis-Rüth and Ulrich Eckhard at the Molecular Biology Institute of Barcelona.

Using techniques that measure how molecules interact, White and the Barcelona team showed that BFT and claudin-4 form a tightly bound complex in laboratory experiments. Each toxin molecule paired with one receptor molecule, providing direct physical evidence of the connection.

A Clever Molecular Decoy Blocks the Dangerous Gut Toxin

Identifying the receptor did more than explain how the toxin works. It also gave the scientists an idea for stopping it.

If BFT needs claudin-4 to attach to colon cells, perhaps a substitute could lure the toxin away from its intended target.

To test that possibility, the team developed a molecular decoy. This was a soluble protein carrying sequences from claudin-4, designed to attract BFT without allowing it to attack the colon's protective lining.

The researchers then worked with Min Dong's laboratory at Harvard Medical School, including Kang Wang and colleagues, to investigate the approach in mice. These experiments allowed the scientists to examine how the toxin behaves in the more complicated environment of a living intestine.

The results were encouraging. Instead of binding to claudin-4 receptors on colon cells, BFT attached to the decoy proteins. By intercepting the toxin, the decoys successfully protected the mice from BFT-induced damage.

The finding suggests that it may be possible to interfere with the toxin's first step rather than trying to repair the damage after it occurs.

"This approach could be iterated upon with small molecules or other biologics that have better pharmacological properties," says White. The team is now exploring which molecular approaches might be most successful to block the toxin.

Small molecules are compounds that can sometimes be developed into medicines, while biologics are treatments made from or involving biological materials, such as proteins. Future versions of the decoy strategy could potentially be designed to work more effectively in the body or be easier to administer.

What This Discovery Could Mean for Colon Cancer Prevention

Although the findings identify a promising new target, important questions remain.

Scientists have established that BFT attaches to claudin-4 and that blocking this interaction can protect mice from toxin-induced damage. However, they have not yet captured the exact experimental three-dimensional structure showing how the two molecules fit together.

Even advanced artificial intelligence tools, including AlphaFold, have been unable to fully resolve the interaction. Understanding its precise structure could help researchers design more effective compounds that prevent the toxin from binding.

Further experiments will also be needed to determine whether the decoy approach can safely and effectively prevent toxin-related disease in humans. The mouse experiments demonstrated protection against tissue damage, but they did not establish that the strategy prevents colorectal cancer.

Nevertheless, the discovery resolves a major question that has persisted since the connection between BFT and colon tumor formation was established in 2009. By identifying the toxin's previously unknown point of attachment, researchers have uncovered a potential way to interrupt a harmful biological process before it begins.

The findings could ultimately support new strategies for detecting or treating conditions associated with bacterial toxins, including colorectal cancer, diarrhea, and bloodstream infections.

Additional researchers who contributed to the study include Jason Chen, Shaoguang Wu, Abby L. Geis, and Jessica Queen of Johns Hopkins, along with Hailong Zhang, Karthik Hullahalli, and Jie Zhang of Harvard Medical School.

Funding was provided by the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Janssen Research and Development, Cancer Research UK, the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R01 AI042347, R01 NS080833, R01 NS117626, R01 AI170835 and R01 AI189789) and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute.

#5638. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5637. Active Inventory Grows as Sellers Keep Homes on the Market

As the holiday season approaches, housing market activity on both the buyer and seller sides are cooling right along with the temperatures. Moving toward what is typically a slower time for the housing market anyway, a new report shows buyers are holding back as elevated rates continue to diminish their buying power and sellers are bringing fewer homes to market, but not broadly delisting.

According to the Realtor.com’s  October monthly housing report, new listings fell 7.5% year over year, the steepest decline of 2026, while 4.4% of active listings were delisted, compared with 4.6% a year earlier. The preliminary share of listings with price cuts was 20.5%, just 0.2 percentage points above last year and down from September.

Meanwhile, the report shows the number of homes under contract fell 10.5% year over year, the greatest decline in nearly three years, as buyers pulled back.

“The market is cooling on both sides, but in different ways. Buyers are stepping back as higher mortgage rates cut into their buying power, while sellers are listing less often without a broad increase in delistings or price cuts,” said Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “We’re seeing a pause in new supply, but owners who already have homes on the market appear to be largely unphased.”

The national median list price was $415,000 in October, down 2.2% from a year earlier and marking the 12th consecutive month of annual declines. Active inventory grew for a fourth straight month, bringing the national supply gap to 6.7% below typical pre-pandemic levels—the narrowest gap since the pandemic, according to the report.

Realtor.com says the stock of homes under contract fell 10.5% year over year for a third consecutive monthly decline, the steepest annual drop since October 2023. Thirty-year mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, 110 basis points above a year earlier, putting added pressure on buyers’ purchasing power.

At the same time, 357,000 new listings came to market, down 7.5% from October 2025. Despite fewer new listings, active inventory reached 1,183,500 homes, up 7.4% year over year—the fastest annual growth in eight months. The year-over-year acceleration partly reflects a slower inventory comparison last fall; active listings have also risen each month since February. National inventory is now 6.6% below typical pre-pandemic levels, the narrowest gap since the pandemic.

Sellers did not respond to weaker demand with a broad wave of withdrawals, the report shows. The number of delisted homes rose 2.7% year over year, but the delisting rate— delistings as a share of active listings—held at 4.4%, compared with 4.6% a year earlier. The rate ticked up from about 4.0% in September, in line with the typical seasonal rise into fall.

Price cuts remained common, but their share eased from September. 20.5% of active listings saw their prices reduced in October, down 0.3 percentage points from the prior month and 0.2 points above a year earlier. The October share was the highest for the month since 2022 and the second-highest of 2026.

“Rates eased to 7.24% on Oct. 29, down from 7.40% in mid-October, but they remained 107 basis points above a year ago and 53 basis points above early September. That loss of purchasing power is showing up first in demand: The stock of homes under contract is down over 10% year over year, while the rate of contract signings fell 17% year over year,” said Jake Krimmel, senior economist at Realtor.com.

As the market moves into the holiday months, the balance between inventory and prices will be an important test, writes Realtor.com. More homes for sale and slower sales can increase supply, but if sellers do not make deeper price cuts, buyers may not gain as much ground as inventory growth alone suggests.

“On the seller side, we see more of a pause than an exodus,” said Krimmel. “New listings are down at a time of year when activity is already seasonally low, but the share of listings with price cuts is only 0.2 percentage points above last year and slipped from September. We also haven’t seen a meaningful increase in delistings. As we approach the holidays, a seller pulling a listing around Halloween or Thanksgiving is not necessarily showing the same distress as one who exits in midsummer.”

“A well-timed offer with reasonable, season-specific requests has a much higher chance of acceptance when winter is around the corner,” says one real estate pro. Read more.

#5636. Trump Declares the Oval Office a National Monument—1 Year After Backlash Over ‘Home Depot’ Decor

President Donald Trump declared the Oval Office a national monument aiming to stop future presidents from making any changes. Trump signed a proclamation on Thursday in his first official action since Democrats swept the midterms.

"We've had tremendous victory in this office," Trump said. "So we're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape."

Only a year ago, Trump, 80, found himself defending the "24-karat gold" Oval Office decorations as critics speculated they were actually painted plastic appliqués from Home Depot.

"You know the one thing with gold?" Trump said during a Fox News interview with host Laura Ingraham in 2025. "You can't imitate gold, real gold. There's no paint that imitates gold."

Ingraham, 63, then pushed Trump further, asking him: "So these aren't from Home Depot or something?"

"No, this is not Home Depot stuff," the president responded. "This is not Home Depot."

After filming, the Fox News host posted the short clip on her social media accounts, captioning it: "In the Oval Office with President Trump and can confirm that it is REAL gold!"

Trump's confirmation that the additions to the Oval Office are "real gold" comes after a frenzy of speculation broke out online that the White House upgrades were nothing more than cheap imitations designed to mock the appearance of the precious metal.

Many pointed to one particular motif that very closely resembles a $58.07 polyurethane applique that is available on Home Depot's website.

Those rumors were further fueled when a spokesperson for the design company behind the appliques, Ekena Millwork, told Buzzfeed that they believe their products could well have been used in the White House renovations.

"We work with several design firms in DC that have worked on the White House and believe these could be our onlays," the spokesperson said.

Ironically, the design that many believe is identical to the moldings used in the Oval Office has since sold out the Home Depot website.

It is not the first time that Trump's White House renovations have caused a stir online—with some hitting out at the president for his "out of touch" emphasis on aesthetic upgrades at a time of such economic volatility, particular in light of the 2025 government shutdown, which had denied millions their SNAP benefits.

Other critics have slammed Trump for making such significant changes to such a historic room in the White House, particularly after he also made several dramatic updates to the building's facade and structure.

The backlash began in March 2025, just two months after his inauguration, when Trump announced plans to pave over the historic White House Rose Garden, telling reporters that he wanted to make the events space safer for guests, particularly women in heels.

"You know, we use [the Rose Garden] for press conference and it doesn't work because the people fall," he said during a March interview on Fox News. "The terrain can be wet, and the soft ground can be an issue for some. Women, with the high heels, it just didn't work."

Despite the backlash over the plans, Trump pressed on with his redesign of the outdoor space, with images taken in June 2025 revealing that the grass had been ripped up and replaced with gravel.

The completed paved area was later filled with tables, chairs, and yellow-and-white umbrellas that many noted were almost identical to those used poolside at Trump's Florida resort, Mar-a-Lago.

As part of the redesign, the Rose Garden has been outfitted with new drainage systems to prevent water from pooling at its center.

Work on the historic garden began June 9, 2025, when employees of the National Park Service began removing a limestone border that had been installed by Trump's wife, Melania, 56, during his first term in office.

The renovation quickly progressed, with images taken on June 17 and June 18 of last year revealing that the entire lawn had been ripped up by bulldozers—as well as several poles that were under the ground—before gravel was laid across the entire surface.

Despite Trump's insistence that the garden renovation was entirely necessary, the project has sparked some backlash from critics, who insist that the "removal" of such an important piece of White House history is disrespectful.

"White House Rose Garden gone. Absolutely crazy," one such person wrote in a post shared on X.

"To remove Kennedy's Rose Garden is removing a piece of our White House history. And for a patio," another person chimed in.

"Melania and Donald Trump are ruining the White House Rose Garden once again. They're deporables," one other person posted.

However, a White House spokesperson insisted to People that Trump and his wife have "the deepest respect for the history of the White House and the Rose Garden," adding: "This restoration to the Rose Garden preserves the beauty of the space and builds on the work done in 2020, with a focus on enhancing practical use and guest experience for those attending special events."

Trump prompted further fury from critics when it was revealed that his $300 million plan to outfit the White House with a new ballroom would require the complete demolition of the building's East Wing.

Initially, Trump had insisted that the addition of a 90,000-square-foot ballroom at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue would not interfere with the existing structure, telling reporters in July: "It won’t interfere with the current building. It won’t be. It’ll be near it but not touching it—and pays total respect to the existing building, which I’m the biggest fan of."

However, those plans are understood to have changed after a meeting with architects revealed there would not be enough space for the planned ballroom without the destruction of the East Wing.

During his interview with Ingraham, the president once again defended the project, telling the Fox News host that the East Wing "looked like hell" when it was torn down—noting that the ballroom will be a much grander addition to the White House.

"The East Wing was a beautiful, little, tiny structure that was built many years ago that was renovated and expanded and disbanded and columns ripped out—and it had nothing to do with the original building," he said.

"It was a poor, sad sight, and I could have built the ballroom around it, but it would not have been—we’re building one of the greatest ballrooms in the world."

#5635. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. And that could work in your favor.If you're ready to buy, talk to a local agent about which builders have completed homes sitting on the market in your area see what they're willing to offer to get them sold.

#5633. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.
